title: Playbook
text:
-
  Title: Before accepting the role
  Items:
    - What outcome am I accountable for?
    - Who appointed me and where do I report?
    - What may I decide personally?
    - Which matters are retained by formal governance, the Board or another authority?
    - Do I have enough capacity and organisational authority to sponsor this transaction actively?
-
  Title: Before empowering the Transaction Director
  Items:
    - Is the strategic direction and intended end-state clear?
    - Are delegated decisions, budget limits and escalation triggers explicit?
    - Can the Director reach the required senior leaders quickly?
    - Will I support delegated decisions when stakeholders bypass the agreed route?
    - How will we maintain an honest view of risk, value and readiness?
-
  Title: Before an executive review
  Items:
    - What has changed since the last review?
    - Which outcome, milestone or assumption is now at risk?
    - What evidence supports the forecast?
    - Which decisions or commitments are required from the room?
    - Are the correct authorities present?
    - What becomes harder or impossible if the decision waits?

title: Playbook
text:
-
  Title: Before making or sponsoring a decision
  Items:
    - Is the matter within my authority?
    - Is the substantive decision owned by a specialist, country or formal forum?
    - Are strategy, cost, timing, risk, customer, employee and value consequences visible?
    - Are the options genuinely different and executable?
    - What is recommended, and which assumption matters most?
    - Is the decision reversible, conditional or final?
    - How will it be recorded and translated into action?
-
  Title: Before a readiness or go or no-go forum
  Items:
    - Are functional and country recommendations complete?
    - Does accepted evidence support the integrated position?
    - Have cross-workstream and counterparty dependencies been tested?
    - Are material conditions executable and owned?
    - Is residual risk distinguished from unresolved work?
    - Does the Transaction Director provide a clear execution recommendation?
    - Am I ready to sponsor a clear view rather than pass the choice upward?
    - Does the named formal forum retain the final authority?
-
  Title: During cutover and stabilisation
  Items:
    - Is decision authority available at the speed live execution requires?
    - Are customers, employees, controls and critical operations protected?
    - Are conditions and stop triggers visible?
    - Are senior stakeholders receiving one controlled message?
    - Is the programme holding delegated authority, or are routine matters drifting upward?
    - What must be true before executive attention can safely reduce?

title: Playbook
text:
-
  Title: Before programme closure
  Items:
    - Have the intended strategic and operational outcomes been achieved or explicitly rebaselined?
    - Are benefits, costs, obligations and remaining risks owned?
    - Has normal business ownership accepted the handover?
    - Are unresolved transition services and exit dates visible?
    - Have material lessons changed future standards, governance or mobilisation practice?
    - Is closure based on stable outcomes rather than the end of programme reporting?

title: Principles
text:
- Own the outcome, not every task.
- Set clear direction before demanding detailed plans.
- Delegate authority as well as responsibility.
- Protect delegated decisions when they remain within mandate.
- Intervene early when enterprise commitment or authority is required.
- Keep specialist decisions with the specialist authority.
- Test evidence, consequences and assumptions rather than asking for more volume.
- Connect execution choices to strategy, value and risk.
- Make or sponsor decisions before useful options disappear.
- Stay visibly engaged until outcomes are stable and ownership is accepted.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: The Transaction Director has made a decision within agreed scope, budget and risk limits. A senior functional executive asks the Sponsor to reverse it. What should the Sponsor establish first?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: Whether the functional executive has more subject expertise than the Transaction Director.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: Whether the decision remains within delegated authority and aligned to the transaction objectives using the available evidence.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Whether reopening the decision would improve executive alignment without moving the programme date.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: Whether formal governance can consider both positions before execution begins.
  Answer: B
  Feedback: The first test is the mandate and transaction outcome. A Sponsor should not weaken delegated authority merely because a senior stakeholder prefers another executable option.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: A critical workstream cannot secure a specialist because another enterprise programme has a fixed external deadline. What is the Sponsor's main contribution?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: Select which programme receives the specialist using the relative size of each approved budget.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: Ask the Transaction Director to absorb the constraint because workstream capacity sits within execution accountability.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Require an integrated view of both obligations and use enterprise authority to secure a workable priority, capacity or timing decision.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: Refer the matter to the next Executive Committee because both programmes have valid organisational priorities.
  Answer: C
  Feedback: The Sponsor resolves organisational barriers that programme leaders cannot solve alone. The decision should integrate both obligations rather than automatically favouring one programme or forum.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: A policy interpretation threatens a transaction milestone. The Programme Manager has shown the timing and cost effects. Who should determine the policy interpretation?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: The Executive Sponsor, because the issue has become material to the transaction.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: The Transaction Director, because that role owns successful transaction execution.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: The relevant policy or control authority, with the Sponsor accelerating the route and managing the transaction consequences.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: Formal executive governance, because the functional authority has not resolved it within the programme timetable.
  Answer: C
  Feedback: Material programme consequences do not transfer specialist authority. The Sponsor should remove delay and secure the right decision while keeping execution options visible.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: A proposed change remains within the total approved budget but uses nearly all remaining contingency and delays benefit delivery. What information is most important before Sponsor approval?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: Confirmation that Finance can fund the change without requesting additional budget.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: The effect on the business case, strategic outcome, alternatives, uncertainty, authority and future ability to absorb risk.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Agreement from every affected Workstream Executive that the change is the best delivery option.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: A fixed supplier price and a revised integrated plan approved by the Transaction Director.
  Answer: B
  Feedback: Remaining within the total budget is not enough. The Sponsor must understand value, timing, uncertainty, alternatives and the loss of future flexibility.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: What is the correct division of responsibility before a formal go or no-go decision?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: Workstreams provide evidence; the Programme Manager forms the recommendation; the Sponsor makes the final decision.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: Workstreams provide evidence; the Transaction Director accepts the risks; the Sponsor records the final decision for governance.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Workstreams provide evidence; the programme integrates it; the Transaction Director forms the execution recommendation; the Sponsor tests and sponsors it; the authorised forum decides.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: Workstreams provide recommendations; the Sponsor integrates the business view; the Board validates the supporting evidence and decides.
  Answer: C
  Feedback: Each level adds the judgement attached to its mandate. Formal governance retains the final decision where the go or no-go matter is reserved.

title: Resource notice
text: The templates and records named here are not stored in the Capability Hub. Source the current approved versions from the transaction team or controlled programme workspace. Do not create an uncontrolled alternative where an approved version exists.

title: A contested resource commitment
text:
Title: A contested resource commitment
Situation: Six weeks before a major readiness gate, the Technology Executive advises that two specialists committed to the transaction are needed for a regulatory remediation programme. Both initiatives have fixed external deadlines. The Transaction Director proposes moving one specialist and funding a contractor to retain transaction capacity, but Technology believes the contractor will require too much supervision. Neither deadline can yet be moved without senior engagement.
Options:
  -
    Key: A
    Text: Confirm the transaction's existing priority and require Technology to retain both specialists until the readiness gate, leaving the remediation programme to find alternatives.
  -
    Key: B
    Text: Ask the Technology Executive and Transaction Director to produce a time-bound enterprise option that shows both obligations, capability constraints, cost and deadline consequences, then use Sponsor authority to secure the chosen commitment.
  -
    Key: C
    Text: Accept Technology's proposed reassignment because a regulatory programme should take priority, and ask the Transaction Director to replan the readiness gate around the reduced capacity.
  -
    Key: D
    Text: Split each specialist's time equally between the two programmes and require weekly reporting so emerging effects can be managed before either deadline is missed.
Answer: B

title: A contested resource commitment
text: Feedback: Option B treats the conflict as an enterprise decision and creates the information needed to secure a workable commitment. Option A protects the transaction but assumes the other obligation can absorb the loss. Option C gives one valid priority automatic precedence without integrating the consequences. Option D appears balanced but may leave both programmes with insufficient focused capacity.

title: Pressure to overrule a delegated decision
breadcrumb: Pressure to overrule a delegated decision
text:
Title: Pressure to overrule a delegated decision
Situation: The Transaction Director approves a phased customer migration within the agreed scope, budget and risk limits. It lowers cutover concentration but delays some benefits by one month. A Workstream Executive who preferred a single migration contacts you directly and argues that the phased option signals weak ambition. The Programme Manager's analysis supports the Director's decision, although either approach remains executable.
Options:
  -
    Key: A
    Text: Review whether the decision remains within the delegated mandate and aligned to the transaction objectives, then support it unless new evidence changes the strategic or risk position.
  -
    Key: B
    Text: Reopen the decision in the next executive forum because disagreement from a senior functional owner indicates that wider sponsorship is needed.
  -
    Key: C
    Text: Ask the Transaction Director and Workstream Executive to agree a compromise sequence so that both perspectives are reflected before execution begins.
  -
    Key: D
    Text: Select the single migration because the Executive Sponsor should favour the option that realises the approved benefits sooner when both are executable.
Answer: A

title: Pressure to overrule a delegated decision
breadcrumb: Pressure to overrule a delegated decision
text: Feedback: Option A protects clear delegation while preserving Sponsor oversight of strategic alignment. Option B weakens the decision route when the matter remains within mandate. Option C may improve alignment but risks substituting consensus for accountable decision-making. Option D focuses on benefit timing without taking ownership of the execution and risk trade-off already delegated.

title: Scenarios
text:
-
  Title: A specialist decision with programme consequences
  Situation: A proposed data-retention approach would protect the planned customer migration date and remain within budget. Legal and Privacy disagree on whether it meets the required standard. The delay in resolving their interpretation will remove the preferred migration window. The Transaction Director asks you to choose between the two approaches so planning can continue.
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: Choose the more conservative interpretation because it reduces the chance of later regulatory challenge, then ask the programme to recover the timing impact.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: Choose the approach that protects the migration date because the Sponsor owns the overall transaction outcome and both functions have presented defensible views.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Convene the named specialist authorities to resolve or formally escalate the interpretation immediately, while directing the Transaction Director to prepare the execution choices for each possible outcome.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: Pause migration planning until Legal and Privacy reach agreement, because programme pressure should not influence a specialist interpretation.
  Answer: C
  Feedback: Option C keeps the specialist decision with the correct authority while actively managing the transaction deadline and alternatives. Options A and B turn Sponsor accountability into specialist authority. Option D respects the boundary but does not use available executive influence to accelerate a decision before options disappear.

title: A business-case change near commitment
text:
Title: A business-case change near commitment
Situation: A supplier revises its estimate for a required separation activity from R18 million to between R23 million and R26 million. The approved business case contains R8 million of remaining central contingency. Delaying the appointment by two weeks is likely to add three weeks to the programme, but the supplier will not provide a fixed price until discovery is complete. The Transaction Director recommends a capped discovery phase costing R2 million, credited against the final fee, followed by a final commitment decision.
Options:
  -
    Key: A
    Text: Approve the full R26 million estimate now because it remains inside the total business case when contingency is included and protects the programme date.
  -
    Key: B
    Text: Approve the capped discovery phase with explicit outputs, price and timing limits, preserve the later commitment decision, and update the business-case range and programme consequences.
  -
    Key: C
    Text: Require the supplier to provide a fixed price before any further spend because the current range is too wide for responsible executive approval.
  -
    Key: D
    Text: Refer the full supplier appointment to the next formal governance forum because the upper estimate would use all remaining contingency.
Answer: B

title: A business-case change near commitment
text: Feedback: Option B buys information while limiting exposure and preserving a decision point before the larger commitment. Option A treats contingency as automatic approval and commits against an uncertain estimate. Option C protects cost certainty but may create avoidable delay and offers no route to improve the estimate. Option D may eventually be required, but a limited discovery decision can preserve options if it sits within Sponsor authority.

title: A conditional readiness recommendation
text:
Title: A conditional readiness recommendation
Situation: All functional leaders recommend proceeding to Business Day 1. One high-severity operational risk remains: a tested manual process can maintain customer service for four hours if an automated hand-off fails, but recovery beyond four hours has not been demonstrated. The likelihood is assessed as low, the formal risk owner has accepted the exposure within their authority, and the Transaction Director recommends proceeding with a two-hour executive checkpoint after launch. The formal go or no-go forum is tomorrow.
Options:
  -
    Key: A
    Text: Sponsor a proceed recommendation because the risk owner has accepted the exposure and the proposed checkpoint provides additional executive control.
  -
    Key: B
    Text: Sponsor a hold recommendation until recovery beyond four hours has been demonstrated, because customer continuity should not depend on an unproven recovery path.
  -
    Key: C
    Text: Test the failure consequence, monitoring, trigger, decision authority and recovery options; then present an explicit recommendation and conditions to the formal forum rather than treating risk acceptance as the go or no-go decision.
  -
    Key: D
    Text: Present the Transaction Director's recommendation and the functional risk acceptance without a Sponsor view, allowing the formal forum to determine the appropriate balance.
Answer: C

title: A conditional readiness recommendation
text: Feedback: Option C applies Sponsor judgement and preserves the formal forum's decision authority. Option A may become the final recommendation but does not show that the remaining exposure and checkpoint are executable. Option B may also become appropriate, but the information given does not yet show that holding is the only proportionate response. Option D passes information upward without the integrated Sponsor recommendation expected by the forum.

title: Start steps
text:
-
  Title: Confirm the sponsorship mandate
  Good: The appointing authority has confirmed the Sponsor's accountability, reporting route, decision authority and any matters retained by the Board or another formal forum.
  Action: Clarify what success means, what you may decide, what must be sponsored elsewhere and how urgent matters reach the correct authority.
  Evidence: Sponsor appointment, authority statement, reserved-matter list and escalation route.
-
  Title: Align the strategic direction
  Good: The deal rationale, business case, intended end-state, customer and employee outcomes, key obligations and non-negotiable constraints are clear enough to guide execution choices.
  Action: Translate transaction intent into a short set of success criteria and decision principles. Resolve contradictions before detailed planning begins.
  Evidence: Approved direction, success criteria, controlling assumptions and open strategic questions.
-
  Title: Appoint and empower the Transaction Director
  Good: The Transaction Director has suitable experience, sufficient capacity and written authority to mobilise the programme, spend approved budget within limits, resolve execution trade-offs and escalate at short notice.
  Action: Confirm the mandate, decision limits, reporting relationship, access to senior leaders and expectations for transparent escalation.
  Evidence: Role acceptance, delegation statement, budget limits, escalation triggers and agreed success measures.

title: Start steps
text:
-
  Title: Establish accountable leadership
  Good: The Sponsor and Transaction Director have appointed capable Workstream Executives. Leaders understand their outcomes, authority, capacity commitments and responsibility to release suitably skilled team members.
  Action: Resolve senior appointment or capacity gaps and make clear that transaction commitments are organisational commitments, not optional project requests.
  Evidence: Leadership map, role confirmations, capacity commitments, deputies and unresolved gaps.
-
  Title: Set decision and governance routes
  Good: Each formal forum has a clear purpose, authority, membership and output. Urgent issues can be decided outside the meeting calendar without losing control or traceability.
  Action: Approve the governance design, ensure the right authorities participate and test one sample decision and escalation before the programme depends on the route.
  Evidence: Governance terms, decision map, calendar, dry-run result and named escalation contacts.
-
  Title: Secure resources and funding
  Good: The initial programme team, specialist support, supplier capacity and approved funding are sufficient for mobilisation and planning. Constraints are explicit rather than hidden in optimistic assumptions.
  Action: Resolve enterprise resource conflicts, confirm the initial budget and require material capacity gaps to have owners and resolution dates.
  Evidence: Approved mobilisation budget, resource commitments, supplier assumptions and open constraints.

title: Start steps
text:
-
  Title: Align senior stakeholders
  Good: Executive Committee, Board, function and country leaders understand the transaction's importance, confidentiality restrictions, immediate priorities and their expected decisions or support.
  Action: Lead the senior narrative, align stakeholders before formal meetings where possible and prevent conflicting executive messages from reaching the programme.
  Evidence: Stakeholder map, leadership brief, agreed messages, engagement plan and unresolved concerns.
-
  Title: Sponsor the mobilisation gate
  Good: The programme can show that leadership, capacity, tools, governance, controls, interfaces and immediate plans are operational. Open exceptions have named owners, dates and consequences.
  Action: Challenge whether the programme is genuinely ready to deepen planning. Decide or sponsor a decision to proceed, proceed with conditions or hold.
  Evidence: Mobilisation dashboard, gate pack, conditions, decision record and authorised next actions.

title: Success measures
text:
-
  Title: Strategic alignment
  Text: execution remains aligned to the deal rationale, business case and intended operating model.
-
  Title: Decision effectiveness
  Text: material decisions are made at the correct level before options disappear.
-
  Title: Organisational commitment
  Text: leaders provide the people, funding and priority required for delivery.
-
  Title: Transaction outcome
  Text: the intended strategic, commercial and operational objectives remain achievable.
-
  Title: Risk oversight
  Text: material risks are mitigated, accepted by the correct authority or reflected in the transaction decision.
-
  Title: Readiness
  Text: major gates are supported by complete evidence and a clear integrated recommendation.
-
  Title: Value protection
  Text: threats to benefits, costs, customers, employees, obligations and timing are visible and acted upon.
-
  Title: Leadership effectiveness
  Text: the Transaction Director and programme team have clear authority, support and escalation routes.

title: Classify
text:
-
  Prompt: A bank sells a portfolio of home loans to another lender. No staff or systems move.
  Options:
    - Balance-sheet transaction
    - Partial-business transaction
    - Full-business transaction
  Correct: 0
  Feedback:
    - Right. Only specific assets move. The work still includes customer notices and data transfer.
    - Close, but no people, systems or operations move. That makes it balance-sheet only.
    - No entity or whole business moves. Only a set of loans changes hands.
-
  Prompt: A bank buys all the shares of a licensed payments company, with its staff, systems and licence.
  Options:
    - Balance-sheet transaction
    - Partial-business transaction
    - Full-business transaction
  Correct: 2
  Feedback:
    - Much more than assets move here. The whole entity, including its licence, changes owner.
    - It would be partial if only part of the company moved. Here the whole entity moves.
    - Right. The whole entity moves. Licences, people and systems all come with it.
-
  Prompt: A bank sells its card business: customer accounts, the card team and the card platform, but not the rest of the bank.
  Options:
    - Balance-sheet transaction
    - Partial-business transaction
    - Full-business transaction
  Correct: 1
  Feedback:
    - People and a platform move too, so it goes beyond balance-sheet only.
    - Right. One business line moves with its people and systems. Separating shared services is often the hard part.
    - The rest of the bank stays. Only part of the business moves.

title: Classify
text:
-
  Prompt: A bank takes over the deposits and branches of a failing lender, but not its bad loans.
  Options:
    - Balance-sheet transaction
    - Partial-business transaction
    - Full-business transaction
  Correct: 1
  Feedback:
    - Branches and the people who run them move too, so this is more than balance-sheet.
    - Right. A chosen part of the business moves. The perimeter deliberately excludes the bad loans.
    - Not everything moves. The bad loans are excluded, so the perimeter is partial.

title: Closing
text:
-
  Prompt: Which outcomes need stronger evidence first?
  Options:
    - Cost savings, because the whole business case rests on them
    - Customer and service continuity, because payments and fraud defects are still open
    - Regulatory outcomes, because approval depends on financial-crime remediation
  Correct: 1
  Feedback:
    - Savings do need validating, and it matters. But they can be tested after LD1. Payment and fraud failures would harm customers on day one.
    - Strongest choice. Open defects in payments and fraud monitoring put customers and controls at risk immediately. Savings and approval still need evidence, but continuity comes first.
    - A strong case. Without approval there is no deal. But approval is partly outside the team's control, while the defects are within it and affect customers directly.
-
  Prompt: What should be escalated, changed or made a condition of readiness?
  Options:
    - Escalate the late communications and ask for more resource to catch up
    - Make fixing the payment and fraud defects, and completing remediation, conditions of readiness
    - Re-baseline the savings figure so the business case reflects the real perimeter
  Correct: 1
  Feedback:
    - Useful, and it should happen. But it treats a symptom. The defects and remediation are the harder blockers.
    - Strongest choice. It links readiness to evidence on the issues that could harm customers and block approval. Communications and savings still need action.
    - Honest and needed. But re-baselining does not make LD1 any safer for customers.

title: Closing
text:
-
  Prompt: What would you recommend?
  Options:
    - Proceed on the planned date
    - Proceed with conditions
    - Delay
  Correct: 1
  Feedback:
    - Keeping the date protects momentum and cost. But it accepts open defects in payments and fraud monitoring, which risks customers and controls.
    - Strongest choice, if the conditions are firm and evidenced: defects fixed, remediation accepted by the regulator, communications sent in time. If any condition slips, the answer becomes delay.
    - Safe, and sometimes right. But delay has real costs: staff uncertainty, customer confusion and a longer spend. Delay should follow a failed condition, not replace a decision.

title: Closing links
text:
Cost: Savings are not yet validated against the perimeter.
Regulatory: Approval now depends on financial-crime remediation.
Customers: Customer communications are behind plan.
Continuity: Defects affect payments and fraud monitoring.
Tech: Defects affect payments and fraud monitoring.

title: Convert
text:
-
  Activity: Migrate customer data to the new platform.
  Outcome:
    Prompt: Which is the best outcome statement?
    Options:
      - All customer records are loaded onto the new platform by the migration date
      - Customers can transact from LD1 with accurate balances and controls working
      - The migration team completes all planned data loads on schedule
    Correct: 1
    Feedback:
      - Loaded records can still be wrong, or controls can fail. This is closer to an activity.
      - Right. It describes what the customer and the bank need, not just the task.
      - Completing loads is progress on activity. It says nothing about accuracy or customers.
  Evidence:
    Prompt: Which evidence best supports it?
    Options:
      - Reconciled balances, successful dress rehearsal and control test results
      - A signed-off migration plan
      - Status report showing all tasks green
    Correct: 0
    Feedback:
      - Right. This shows the result actually happened.
      - A plan shows intent, not results.
      - Green status can hide gaps. It reports activity, not outcomes.

title: Convert
text:
-
  Activity: Run a staff retention scheme.
  Outcome:
    Prompt: Which is the best outcome statement?
    Options:
      - Retention letters are issued to all staff before signing
      - Morale remains positive throughout the programme
      - At least 90% of named critical staff remain 12 months after completion
    Correct: 2
    Feedback:
      - Issuing letters is an activity. People may still leave.
      - Morale matters but is hard to measure and not tied to critical roles.
      - Right. It is measurable, targeted and timed.
  Evidence:
    Prompt: Which evidence best supports it?
    Options:
      - Monthly count of critical staff still in role, tracked against the named list
      - Number of retention letters signed
      - Engagement survey response rate
    Correct: 0
    Feedback:
      - Right. It measures the outcome directly.
      - Signed letters show take-up, not whether people stay.
      - Response rate says little about retention.

title: Defs
text:
Due diligence: A detailed review of a business before a deal is agreed. It checks finances, customers, contracts, risks and controls.
Synergy: An extra financial benefit created by combining or separating businesses, such as lower costs or more revenue.
Deal perimeter: What is included in, and excluded from, the transaction.
Ld1: Legal Day 1. The point at which legal ownership or agreed legal obligations take effect.
Cutover: The planned, controlled switch from old arrangements to new ones, such as moving accounts to a new system.
Hypercare: A short period after cutover with extra support to spot and fix issues quickly before normal teams take over.
Operational resilience: The ability to keep important services running, or restore them quickly, when something goes wrong.
Regulatory approval: Formal permission from a regulator that a deal can go ahead. Some deals cannot complete without it.
Business as usual: The normal, ongoing teams and processes that run the business after the programme ends.
Financial crime: Money laundering, fraud, sanctions breaches and similar offences. Banks must have controls to prevent them.

title: Matches
text:
-
  Rationale: Buy a digital lender to gain its app and technology team.
  Value:
    Prompt: Main value sought
    Options:
      - Specialist capability
      - Lower duplicated costs
      - Released capital
    Correct: 0
    Feedback:
      - Right. The value is the capability, which sits largely in people and systems.
      - Costs may fall later, but that is not why you buy a technology team.
      - Buying uses capital rather than releasing it.
  Risk:
    Prompt: Principal risk
    Options:
      - Key people leave after the deal
      - Regulators reject the brand name
      - Branch closures upset customers
    Correct: 0
    Feedback:
      - Right. If the team leaves, much of the capability leaves with it.
      - Brand issues are possible but rarely the main threat to this value.
      - A digital lender is unlikely to have branches to close.

title: Matches
text:
-
  Rationale: Merge two regional banks with overlapping branches and head offices.
  Value:
    Prompt: Main value sought
    Options:
      - Market entry
      - Lower duplicated costs
      - Diversified funding
    Correct: 1
    Feedback:
      - Both banks are already in the region, so this is not market entry.
      - Right. Overlap creates cost synergy from removing duplication.
      - Funding may improve slightly, but overlap points to cost savings.
  Risk:
    Prompt: Principal risk
    Options:
      - Savings harm service and customers leave
      - The loan book is too small
      - Too few products to cross-sell
    Correct: 0
    Feedback:
      - Right. Cutting too fast can lose customers and wipe out the savings.
      - Size of the loan book is not the main threat to cost savings.
      - Cross-sell matters for revenue, not the cost case.

title: Matches
text:
-
  Rationale: Sell a non-core insurance business to focus on banking.
  Value:
    Prompt: Main value sought
    Options:
      - Revenue growth
      - Released capital and focus
      - New licences
    Correct: 1
    Feedback:
      - Selling usually reduces revenue. The aim is focus and capital.
      - Right. The seller frees capital and management time.
      - The seller gives up licences rather than gaining them.
  Risk:
    Prompt: Principal risk
    Options:
      - Shared services are hard to separate, leaving stranded costs
      - The buyer's app is poor
      - Deposit customers switch banks
    Correct: 0
    Feedback:
      - Right. Costs left behind after separation can erode the benefit.
      - The buyer's app is mainly the buyer's concern.
      - Deposit customers are less directly affected by an insurance sale.

title: Modules
text:
-
  Id: opening
  No: 1
  Title: Would this deal create value?
  Minutes: 4
  Summary: An opening scenario. Choose and rank what you would investigate first.
  Takeaway: Every question here is credible. Deciding what matters most is the real skill. You will return to this deal in Module 7.

title: Modules
text:
-
  Id: what-is-ma
  No: 2
  Title: What M&A is
  Minutes: 4
  Summary: Mergers, acquisitions, divestments and what actually transfers.
  Screens:
    -
      Title: Three kinds of deal
      Body: M&A stands for mergers and acquisitions.

- Acquisition: one firm buys all or part of another.

- Merger: two firms combine into one.

- Divestment: a firm sells or exits part of its business.

Absa can be the buyer or the seller.
    -
      Title: What can transfer
      Body: A banking deal is rarely just a change of owner. It can transfer:

shares · businesses · loan books · deposits · customers · employees · systems · licences · contracts · assets · liabilities

Most deals transfer a mixture of these. Each one needs its own plan.
    -
      Title: How much is transferring
      Body: - Balance-sheet transaction: specific assets or liabilities move, such as a loan book.

- Partial-business transaction: part of a business moves, such as one product line with its people and systems.

- Full-business transaction: a whole business or entity moves.

The deal perimeter sets out exactly what is in and out.
    -
      Title: Signing is not the end
      Body: Signing the agreement starts the hardest part.

Value is realised through execution, transition and sustained business performance. A well-priced deal can still lose value if it is poorly delivered.
  Takeaway: Know what is actually transferring. The perimeter drives the work, the risks and the cost.

title: Modules
text:
-
  Id: why-banks
  No: 3
  Title: Why banks undertake M&A
  Minutes: 4
  Summary: The reasons behind deals, and why banking deals carry extra weight.
  Screens:
    -
      Title: Common reasons
      Body: - Enter a new market or geography.

- Gain customers, products, technology, licences or specialist skills.

- Increase scale and spread fixed costs.

- Create revenue through more products or wider reach.

- Reduce duplicated operating costs.

- Diversify revenue, funding or credit exposure.

- Exit a non-core business or release capital.

- Acquire a distressed business while protecting financial stability.
    -
      Title: Synergy
      Body: Many deals are justified by synergy.

Cost synergy comes from removing duplication, such as two head offices. Revenue synergy comes from selling more, such as offering cards to new customers.

Synergies are estimates. They only become real through delivery.
    -
      Title: Why banking deals matter more
      Body: Banking deals can affect:

deposits · payments · lending · customer data · capital · liquidity · financial-crime controls · regulatory permissions · critical services · confidence in the bank

A mistake can harm customers and the wider financial system, not just the deal.
  Takeaway: Each rationale carries a matching risk. Name both before you commit.

title: Modules
text:
-
  Id: outcomes
  No: 4
  Title: From deal rationale to outcomes
  Minutes: 4
  Summary: Activities are not outcomes. Learn to say what success looks like.
  Screens:
    -
      Title: Activities are not outcomes
      Body: An activity is something you do. An outcome is the result you need.

Activity: move accounts to the new platform.

Outcome: move accounts accurately without disrupting customer access or weakening controls.

Activity: close duplicated sites.

Outcome: deliver sustainable cost savings while keeping customer access and service.
    -
      Title: Six types of outcome
      Body: - Strategic: market position, capability gained.

- Customer: retention, service continuity.

- Financial: revenue, cost savings, integration costs, capital, funding.

- Operational: operational resilience, stable services.

- Risk and regulatory: control effectiveness, approvals met.

- People and capability: employee retention, skills kept.
    -
      Title: Good outcomes are measurable
      Body: A good outcome has a measure, an owner, a date and evidence.

"Improve retention" is vague. "Keep at least 95% of transferred deposit balances six months after LD1, owned by the Retail lead" can be tracked.
  Takeaway: Write outcomes you could prove. If you cannot name the evidence, it is not yet an outcome.

title: What good looks like
text:
Id: good
No: 5
Title: What good looks like
Minutes: 5
Summary: Connected principles of good execution, with two public examples.
Screens:
  -
    Title: Connected principles
    Body: - A clear rationale with realistic assumptions.

- Measurable outcomes, owners, timing and evidence.

- Early engagement with regulators and control functions.

- A credible business and integration plan.

- Clear accountability and decision rights.

- An honest view of perimeter, dependencies and cost.

- Protection of customers, critical services, data and controls.

- Joint planning across business and technology.

- Evidence-based testing, readiness criteria and fallback plans.

- Active value tracking after completion.
  -
    Title: Example: DBS and Citi Taiwan
    Body: DBS completed the integration of Citi's Taiwan consumer-banking business over a planned weekend in August 2023.

It illustrates coordinated cutover, careful sequencing and operational preparation.

This example shows specific execution principles. It is not a claim that every aspect of the deal succeeded.
  -
    Title: Example: JPMorgan Chase and First Republic
    Body: When JPMorgan Chase assumed First Republic Bank's deposits in May 2023, its 84 offices reopened during normal business hours. Customers kept access to their deposits.

It illustrates customer and service continuity in a time-critical transaction.

This example shows specific execution principles. It is not a claim that every aspect of the deal succeeded.
Takeaway: Good execution is a set of linked habits. Missing one often weakens the others.

title: Phases
text:
-
  Phase: Due Diligence
  Pitfall: Unclear perimeter, weak data, hidden control or asset-quality issues, benefits based on optimistic assumptions.
  Warning: Data requests stay open; benefit figures are not traced to evidence.
  Action: Agree the perimeter early and test key assumptions against data.
-
  Phase: Legal Drafting and Signature
  Pitfall: Commitments that do not reflect operational reality; unclear data-sharing, regulatory, service or transitional arrangements.
  Warning: Operations teams have not reviewed the draft terms.
  Action: Have delivery owners check every operational commitment before signing.
-
  Phase: Mobilisation and Planning
  Pitfall: Late appointments, unclear authority, insufficient capacity, plans listing activities without outcomes, evidence or dependencies.
  Warning: Key roles are unfilled; plans have no owners or evidence.
  Action: Appoint accountable owners and build outcome-based plans.
-
  Phase: Programme Execution
  Pitfall: Unresolved dependencies, scope drift, slow decisions, delivery disconnected from the business case.
  Warning: Decisions wait weeks; scope grows without a change process.
  Action: Track dependencies and decisions; tie changes back to the business case.
-
  Phase: Business Testing
  Pitfall: Incomplete coverage, weak evidence, testing activity mistaken for readiness.
  Warning: High pass rates but untested critical journeys.
  Action: Test against critical services and set clear exit criteria.

title: Phases
text:
-
  Phase: Client Onboarding and LD1 Readiness
  Pitfall: Poor product mapping, late customer or employee communications, data, contractual or control gaps, financial-crime requirements not ready.
  Warning: Customer letters not drafted; screening not configured.
  Action: Map products early and plan communications against LD1.
-
  Phase: Dress Rehearsals
  Pitfall: Unrealistic runbooks, unclear command structures, untested fallback arrangements.
  Warning: Rehearsals overrun; nobody has practised rollback.
  Action: Rehearse the full runbook, including the fallback.
-
  Phase: Go/No-Go
  Pitfall: Optimism overriding evidence, unclear acceptance criteria, unresolved material defects.
  Warning: Criteria are changed to fit the date.
  Action: Fix criteria in advance and decide on evidence.
-
  Phase: Cutover
  Pitfall: Unclear authority, uncontrolled change, poor communications, customer or service disruption.
  Warning: Last-minute changes; unclear who can stop the cutover.
  Action: Freeze change and name one command structure.
-
  Phase: Hypercare
  Pitfall: Prolonged dependence on the programme team, weak transfer to business-as-usual owners, poor issue prioritisation, value tracking stopping too early.
  Warning: Programme staff still fix daily issues months later.
  Action: Set exit criteria and hand over to business-as-usual owners with value tracking.

title: Rank limit
text: Rank limit: 5

title: Northbank acquires Meridian Finance
text:
Title: Northbank acquires Meridian Finance
Facts:

title: Five days to the final country rehearsal
breadcrumb: In-country PMO pathway — modules and exercises
Five days to the final country rehearsal
text:
Title: Five days to the final country rehearsal
Intro: The final rehearsal is next week. You know that:
Facts:
  - the central interface is forecast one day late, but remains within the overall schedule buffer;
  - country operations have enough staff for the rehearsal, but not yet for live cutover;
  - a customer notice meets the central date, but local legal review has found wording that may need to change; and
  - a recurring defect has a workaround, although the control owner has not accepted the remaining risk.
Close: The Central Hub has asked for the country's readiness view.
Improved: You are now applying the In-country PMO role through clear local ownership, controlled hand-offs and balanced evidence.
Review: You have completed the pathway. Review the highlighted module before using the playbook on a live transaction.

title: Capstone decisions
breadcrumb: In-country PMO pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: handoff
  Question: How should the late interface and schedule buffer be controlled?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Accept the one-day slip because it is within buffer, and review it again if the forecast moves further.
      Feedback: The buffer covers it today, but without a trigger nobody knows when to act.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Agree the delivered content, acceptance standard and a recovery trigger with the sending team, and record them.
      Feedback: Recommended. It turns a forecast into a controlled hand-off with a clear point to act.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Move local rehearsal activities back by one day now so the country keeps its own buffer intact.
      Feedback: Changes the plan before recovery is tested and may affect other workstreams.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Ask the Central Hub to own the interface date while the country focuses on its own readiness.
      Feedback: The Central Hub coordinates, but the country must still control its side of the hand-off.
  Answer: b
  Reasoning: A shared date is not a controlled hand-off until both sides agree what will be delivered, accepted and when to act.

title: Capstone decisions
breadcrumb: In-country PMO pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: status
  Question: How should the capacity position affect local status?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Keep green, because staff are sufficient for the rehearsal and live cutover capacity can be sorted next.
      Feedback: Rehearsal capacity is not live readiness.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Report the live-cutover capacity gap, its effect on customers and service, the plan to close it and the date it must close.
      Feedback: Recommended. It shows the real operational forecast and the action needed.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Report red, because live cutover cannot happen without enough operational staff.
      Feedback: Sets severity before testing whether the gap can be closed in time.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Leave capacity out of status and raise it with the Operations Lead directly, as it is a local resourcing matter.
      Feedback: Handling it locally is fine, but hiding it from status misstates readiness.
  Answer: b
  Reasoning: Country reporting should show what is really ready, including operations, not only whether rehearsal and technology are on track.

title: Capstone decisions
breadcrumb: In-country PMO pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: mandate
  Question: How should the customer notice proceed while the legal review is unresolved?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Issue it on the central date, as the change may not be needed, and send a correction later if required.
      Feedback: Sending wording Legal has queried takes a reserved decision locally.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Change the wording yourself to what local Legal suggests, so the notice can still go on the central date.
      Feedback: The PMO does not interpret or finalise legal wording.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Prepare the notice for release, ask Legal for a decision by the last workable date, and show the risk to the central date.
      Feedback: Recommended. It keeps momentum while the right authority decides.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Hold the notice indefinitely until Legal and the Central Hub both confirm the final wording.
      Feedback: Protects accuracy, but without a deadline the central date is quietly lost.
  Answer: c
  Reasoning: Lead what the country can own and make the reserved decision, and its deadline, explicit.

title: Capstone decisions
breadcrumb: In-country PMO pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: plan
  Question: What readiness recommendation and escalation should the country make?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Ready, because the defect has a workaround and the country team is confident it can manage it.
      Feedback: The remaining risk has not been accepted by its owner.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Not ready, and ask the Central Hub to postpone the rehearsal until every gap is closed.
      Feedback: Pre-empts a decision that belongs to governance and ignores what is ready.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Ready with conditions, set by the country, with the defect workaround accepted locally until hypercare.
      Feedback: Accepting material risk is reserved, whatever the country's maturity.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: A recommendation showing what is evidenced, what is not, and escalating the defect risk to its control owner for a decision.
      Feedback: Recommended. It gives a balanced, evidence-based view and routes the risk correctly.
  Answer: d
  Reasoning: The In-country PMO recommends local readiness from balanced evidence. It does not approve it or accept material risk.

title: Context notes
breadcrumb: In-country PMO pathway — modules and exercises
text:
Supported:
  Support: In supported delivery, you supply local facts, access and logistics, while the Central Hub and functional spokes give more hands-on planning and leadership.
  Playbook: Which activities has the centre agreed to lead, and is that split written down?
  Capstone: In supported delivery, you may lean on central teams to do more of this work, but the facts and the local view still come from the country.
Joint:
  Support: In joint delivery, you lead defined local activities and produce evidence, while central and functional teams set standards, challenge outputs and help on complex matters.
  Playbook: Which local activities do we lead, and where are central teams challenging or co-delivering?
  Capstone: In joint delivery, you lead the local response and evidence, with central teams challenging and helping on the complex parts.
Local:
  Support: In locally led delivery, you drive local planning, execution, decision papers and readiness evidence, while central teams challenge and keep the work aligned with the Group.
  Playbook: Where does our delegated authority stop, and which reserved decisions still go to central or specialist owners?
  Capstone: In locally led delivery, you drive the response yourself, but reserved decisions still sit with central or specialist owners.

title: Defect options
breadcrumb: In-country PMO pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Id: a
  Text: Keep the defect open for the second rehearsal, and let the cutover manager decide whether the step stays in scope.
  Feedback: Recognises the cutover manager's role but delays the readiness decision.
-
  Id: b
  Text: Ask the seller for an urgent response and prepare to log the same defect again if the data misses the window.
  Feedback: May get the data but does not protect Absa's processing time.
-
  Id: c
  Text: Set the last workable arrival time, escalate seller approval and Absa processing together, and agree the rehearsal treatment now.
  Feedback: Recommended. It manages the whole chain before the window closes.
-
  Id: d
  Text: Remove the affected step from the second rehearsal so the rest of the runbook can still show progress.
  Feedback: Possibly right, but only once the evidence gap has been assessed through the proper route.

title: Defect situation
breadcrumb: In-country PMO pathway — modules and exercises
text: The first dress rehearsal found a data defect jointly owned by Absa and the seller. The seller must approve and send a corrected extract; Absa then needs four days to process it. Five days before the second rehearsal, seller approval is still outstanding.

title: Three weeks to the next SteerCo
breadcrumb: In-country PMO pathway — modules and exercises
Three weeks to the next SteerCo
text:
Title: Three weeks to the next SteerCo
Intro: The country plan is reported green, but:
Facts:
  - the legal handover arrived late, and two obligations have not been translated into local actions;
  - Technology and the country use the same interface date but describe different outputs;
  - customer communication and frontline training are not included in the readiness evidence; and
  - a Group decision is blocking a local activity, although it appears only in meeting notes.
Close: The next country status submission is due this week.
Message: Several choices can look reasonable from a country seat. The modules show how local ownership, reserved decisions, hand-off control and balanced evidence decide the best response.

title: Diagnostic decisions
breadcrumb: In-country PMO pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: mandate
  Question: Under your operating context, what does the country own in this position?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: The local plan, actions and evidence, and raising the Group decision and obligation questions to the right owners.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Only local logistics and facts, because the Central Hub owns the programme plan and all readiness reporting.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: The whole position, including interpreting the two obligations, since the country knows local law best.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: The local plan and the Group decision, which the country can make itself if the blocker delays local work.
  Answer: a
-
  Capability: plan
  Question: What would make the local plan complete?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Add the two obligations as milestones using the dates in the legal handover, and review them later with Legal.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Ask Legal to explain the two obligations in delivery terms, then add owned local actions and add customer and training evidence to readiness.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Hold the plan as it is until the next readiness review, when Legal and the Central Hub can confirm what is missing.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Add customer communication and training milestones, and leave the obligations with Legal until they are ready to share.
  Answer: b

title: Diagnostic decisions
breadcrumb: In-country PMO pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: handoff
  Question: How should you confirm the Technology hand-off?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Keep the shared date, since both plans match, and note the different descriptions as a risk to monitor.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Update the local plan to match Technology's description so that both plans say the same thing.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Agree with Technology what will be delivered, in what format and standard, who accepts it and what happens if it is late.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Ask the Central Hub to decide which description is right and follow its answer in the local plan.
  Answer: c
-
  Capability: status
  Question: How should you report and escalate the combined position?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Keep green, because no milestone is late, and add the gaps to the commentary for the readiness review.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Report red across the country, because four separate gaps together show the plan cannot be trusted.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Report the technology position as green and the customer position separately, so each owner can act on their part.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Report the forecast against the review with each gap and owner, and escalate the Group decision with its local effect and a date.
  Answer: d

title: Handoff options

text:

  Id: a
  Text: Nothing material. Both lines share the date and describe the same interface.
  Feedback: Matching dates do not prove the same thing is being delivered.
-
  Id: b
  Text: The country expects an approved, load-ready file; the central line only commits to the interface being live.
  Feedback: Recommended. The content and acceptance standard differ, so the hand-off is not yet controlled.
-
  Id: c

-
  Id: d

  Feedback: Worth fixing, but not the gap that would break the hand-off.

  Text: Keeping the local RAID log, actions and decisions current

title: Status options
breadcrumb: In-country PMO pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Id: a
  Text: Green. All technology milestones are on plan, and customer activities are tracked as separate readiness actions.

title: Between rehearsals
Boundary
text: interpreting the sale and purchase agreement (SPA), Group policy, specialist functional approval, the combined programme plan, the transaction business case, transaction-wide budget decisions, the formal go or no-go decision, or reporting to senior leaders.

title: Boundary owns
text: Boundary owns: The country does own explaining how those decisions, commitments and assumptions affect local delivery.

title: Contexts
text:
-
  Id: supported
  Name: Supported delivery
  Text: The country has limited transaction experience, specialist skills, formally authorised decision-making power or spare capacity. The local PMO (programme management office, the team that maintains plans, reporting and delivery controls) supplies facts, access and local logistics. The Central Hub and functional spokes give more hands-on planning, standards and leadership.
-
  Id: joint
  Name: Joint delivery
  Text: The country has capable day-to-day specialists and some transaction experience. The local PMO leads defined local activities and produces evidence. Central and functional teams set standards, challenge outputs and help deliver complex matters.
-
  Id: local
  Name: Locally led delivery
  Text: The country has experienced leads, reliable controls, strong evidence and formally authorised decision-making power. The local PMO drives local planning, execution, decision papers and readiness evidence. Central teams challenge the work, keep it aligned with the Group and escalate specialist matters.

title: Context warning
text: Country maturity changes how much delivery the country can own. It does not hand the country authority over scope, budget, Legal Day 1 (LD1, when legal ownership changes), the Transitional Services Agreement (TSA, temporary services provided after the deal completes), the go or no-go decision (whether it is safe to proceed), Group policy, or accepting a risk that remains after controls are applied.

title: Control rhythm
text:
-
  Title: Refresh the local position
  Text: Update the local plan, milestones, RAID log, dependencies, actions, decisions, resources and evidence. Confirm actual progress with the people doing the work.
-
  Title: Test the customer and operational view
  Text: Check whether technology progress is matched by customer journeys, communications, onboarding, training, operational processes, controls and local service readiness.
-
  Title: Resolve local matters
  Text: Use the authority the country has been given, and country governance, to solve issues that belong locally. Do not send every operational matter to the centre.
-
  Title: Reconcile with the programme
  Text: Align local milestones, dependencies and forecasts with the Central Hub and functional spokes. Find where the same plan item is being read differently.
-
  Title: Escalate complete problems
  Text: For Group, functional or counterparty blockers, provide the facts, local impact, options, your recommendation, who needs to decide, and the last date a decision can still work.
-
  Title: Close the loop
  Text: Bring decisions back into the local plan, confirm the affected teams understand them, and keep evidence of actions, acceptance and closure.

title: Core resources
text:
-
  Name: Regional Spoke operating-model section
  Purpose: Explains country maturity, what the country owns, what must stay central, and the support model you should expect.
  When: During mobilisation and whenever local versus central ownership is unclear.
-
  Name: Country transaction summary and obligation map
  Purpose: Turns the deal perimeter, obligations, restrictions and dates into local delivery implications, without replacing legal or specialist interpretation.
  When: At handover, during mobilisation and when new commitments emerge.
-
  Name: Country maturity and capacity assessment
  Purpose: Tests transaction experience, functional skills, decision authority, spare capacity, governance and evidence capability.
  When: Before agreeing the country delivery model and when capacity or ownership changes.
-
  Name: Local impact assessment
  Purpose: Identifies effects on customers, employees, products, processes, technology, data, controls, suppliers and local entities.
  When: During mobilisation, design and readiness planning.
-
  Name: Country RACI and interface directory
  Purpose: Records who is central, functional, local or counterparty owner, their contacts, deputies and escalation routes.
  When: During mobilisation and whenever a hand-off or authority is disputed.
-
  Name: Local level-2 plan
  Purpose: Makes local activities, owners, dates, resources, dependencies and acceptance criteria deliverable in practice.
  When: Maintain throughout planning, execution, readiness, cutover and handover.

title: Core resources
text:
-
  Name: Local RAID, action, decision and dependency logs
  Purpose: Give traceable local ownership, escalation, ageing and closure.
  When: Maintain continuously and reconcile with programme controls.
-
  Name: Country status report
  Purpose: Gives an evidence-based view of local forecast, customer and operational readiness, exceptions and decisions needed.
  When: At the agreed programme cadence and when material conditions change.
-
  Name: Customer journey and stakeholder map
  Purpose: Stops technology delivery from hiding the real customer, employee and service experience.
  When: During impact assessment, readiness planning and local communications or training design.
-
  Name: Local readiness evidence index
  Purpose: Links local criteria, evidence owners, approvals, gaps and sign-off status.
  When: From planning through go-or-no-go preparation and BAU handover.
-
  Name: Previous transaction lessons and country playbooks
  Purpose: Reuses proven controls, common pitfalls and practical delivery lessons, without assuming two transactions have identical requirements.
  When: During mobilisation, rehearsal planning and issue prevention. Check every reused assumption against the current deal.

title: Economics
Firefighting
text:
-
  Title: Stabilise
  Text: Protect customers, operations and critical deadlines. Confirm who owns the issue right now and what the facts are.
-
  Title: Route
  Text: Resolve it within local authority, or escalate it with a complete decision request. Do not let urgency hide who owns the decision.
-
  Title: Prevent recurrence
  Text: Update the plan, RAID log, evidence and the underlying control so the same issue does not come back through another workstream or rehearsal.

title: Glossary
text:
-
  Term: PMO (programme management office)
  Def: The team that maintains planning, reporting and delivery controls.
-
  Term: Central Hub
  Def: The central Inorganic Change team that coordinates the overall programme.
-
  Term: Functional Spoke
  Def: The central specialist team for a function.
-
  Term: Regional Spoke
  Def: The country or regional team responsible for local input and delivery.
-
  Term: Delegated authority
  Def: The decisions a role has been formally authorised to make.
-
  Term: Reserved decision
  Def: A decision that must remain with a named senior, central or specialist authority.
-
  Term: RAID
  Def: Risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies.
-
  Term: Dependency
  Def: An input, decision or activity that another task relies on.
-
  Term: Residual risk
  Def: Risk that remains after the agreed controls or actions have been applied.
-
  Term: Readiness evidence
  Def: Proof that the required people, processes, technology, data and controls are ready.
-
  Term: Acceptance criteria
  Def: The conditions that must be met before an output is accepted as complete.
-
  Term: Escalation
  Def: Raising a matter to someone with the authority or support needed to resolve it.
-
  Term: Cutover
  Def: The controlled move from the current state to the new operating state.
-
  Term: Runbook
  Def: The timed plan of cutover activities, owners, dependencies and fallback actions.
-
  Term: Dress rehearsal
  Def: A practice run of the cutover plan before live execution.

title: Glossary
text:
-
  Term: Go or no-go
  Def: The formal decision on whether the transaction is ready and safe to proceed.
-
  Term: Hypercare
  Def: The period of increased monitoring and support immediately after cutover.
-
  Term: Business as usual (BAU)
  Def: When ongoing ownership returns to normal teams.
-
  Term: Legal Day 1 (LD1)
  Def: When legal ownership or control changes.
-
  Term: TSA (Transitional Services Agreement)
  Def: Temporary services provided after completion.
-
  Term: Baseline
  Def: The approved plan, budget or scope against which progress is measured.

title: Handoff test
text:
- What exactly will be delivered?
- In what format and to which standard?
- Who produces it and who accepts it?
- What is the committed date and time?
- What evidence confirms completion and acceptance?
- What happens if the hand-off is late or incomplete?

text:
-

  Intensity: Targeted but important
  Level: 2

-
  Period: Mobilisation and planning
  Intensity: Highest
  Level: 4
  Text: Close the knowledge gap, confirm ownership and capacity, map local impact and build the local plan.
-
  Period: Programme execution
  Intensity: Highest
  Level: 4

-
  Period: Testing and dress rehearsals
  Intensity: High
  Level: 3

-
  Period: Readiness and cutover
  Intensity: Highest
  Level: 4

-
  Period: Hypercare and handover
  Intensity: Medium to high
  Level: 3
  Text: Coordinate local issue closure, service stability, remaining actions and BAU acceptance.
