title: Playbook
text:
-
  Title: When joining the transaction
  Items:
    - Do we understand the deal perimeter, dates and affected local entities?
    - Have due diligence findings and signed obligations been translated into delivery language by the right authority?
    - Are local information gaps and assumptions recorded?
    - Is the country's maturity, capacity and delegated authority understood?
    - Are country leadership, workstream owners and deputies confirmed?
    - Is the central, functional and local ownership split documented?
-
  Title: Before accepting the local plan
  Items:
    - Does it cover customers, employees, operations and controls as well as technology?
    - Are activities, owners, resources and dates deliverable locally?
    - Are central, functional and counterparty hand-offs fully defined?
    - Are local regulatory and supplier lead times reflected?
    - Are acceptance criteria and evidence needs explicit?
    - Are testing, rehearsal, cutover, hypercare and BAU handover included early enough?
-
  Title: Before a working group or status submission
  Items:
    - Have local facts been confirmed with the people doing the work?
    - Does status reflect the forecast outcome and evidence, not just activity?
    - Which matters can country governance resolve?
    - Which Group or counterparty blockers need Central Hub coordination?
    - What decision is needed, from whom, and by when?
    - Are customer, operational and cost impacts visible?

title: Playbook
text:
-
  Title: Before confirming a joint hand-off
  Items:
    - Do both parties agree what will be delivered?
    - Are format, quality and acceptance criteria explicit?
    - Are the producer, receiver and decision owners named?
    - Is the date precise and supported by the actions that must happen first?
    - Is completion evidence defined?
    - Is the recovery and escalation route agreed?
-
  Title: Between rehearsals
  Items:
    - Has every defect been classified and assigned?
    - Are seller, Absa and joint dependencies distinguished?
    - Are data, access and approval lead times protected?
    - Is the last workable fix date visible?
    - Has closure evidence been reviewed, not just assumed?
    - Will the next rehearsal test progress rather than rediscover the same issue?
-
  Title: Before local readiness sign-off
  Items:
    - Are customer journeys and operational processes usable end to end?
    - Are people, training, communications, technology, data and controls ready?
    - Are local regulatory commitments and approvals evidenced?
    - Are remaining risks, workarounds and expiry dates explicit?
    - Are local cutover tasks, fallbacks and escalation routes workable?
    - Can the Central Hub trace the evidence behind the country's recommendation?

title: Principles
text:
- Get involved early enough to shape commitments that can actually be delivered.
- Have the right authority translate legal and programme language.
- Keep the customer and local operation next to the technology plan.
- Own as much local delivery as your capability and authority allow.
- Use the centre to unblock the country, not to replace it.
- Define every hand-off beyond just its milestone date.
- Fix defects between rehearsals, not during the next one.
- Escalate complete facts before recovery options run out.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: A high-maturity country has the skills and authority to lead local testing. The test reveals a possible breach of a Group control standard. Who should own the next steps?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: The country owns both the interpretation of the control and the fix, because local testing was delegated to it.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: The Central Hub takes over testing because a Group standard has become relevant to readiness.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: The country owns the local facts, evidence and fix, while the relevant functional or control authority decides the Group-standard position.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: The issue goes straight to the senior decision-making forum, because country delegation no longer applies once a control concern appears.
  Answer: C
  Feedback: Local maturity supports owning execution and evidence. It does not automatically give the country authority to interpret a Group standard or accept a risk that must stay with a central or specialist authority.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: A legal commitment seems relevant to local customer notices, but the country cannot confidently interpret its wording. The notice-planning window has already started. What is the best first response?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: Use the most cautious reading in the local plan until Legal advises otherwise.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: Ask for an authoritative delivery translation and start reversible preparation against a clearly recorded assumption.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Remove the item from planning until the legal position is confirmed, to protect the plan from unsupported content.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: Ask the Central Hub to choose the planning interpretation so local teams can carry on.
  Answer: B
  Feedback: The country should not make the legal judgement itself, but it can save delivery time through open, reversible preparation while the authorised interpretation is obtained.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: A country activity is blocked only by a Group approval. Which statement best describes the ownership split?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: The Central Hub becomes accountable for the whole activity because it coordinates Group functions.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: The country keeps the delivery outcome, the functional owner decides the reserved matter, and the Central Hub coordinates the dependency and escalation.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: The functional owner becomes accountable for local execution until the approval is complete.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: The country should use normal business approval routes before bringing the matter into programme governance.
  Answer: B
  Feedback: A central blocker does not automatically transfer the local outcome. The programme should keep delivery ownership, decision authority and escalation coordination separate.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: Technology is on plan, but customer onboarding evidence is incomplete and the recovery window is narrowing. How should country status be decided?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: From the combined forecast for the required local outcome, showing the evidence gap and the decision date clearly.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: From the technology milestone, because it is the main dependency for onboarding.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: From the most cautious workstream rating until all local evidence is complete.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: By the Central Hub, because it owns combined readiness and reporting to senior leaders.
  Answer: A
  Feedback: The country should give an honest local readiness forecast. The Central Hub combines that view with others, but it cannot create the underlying customer evidence or the local judgement.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: A seller deliverable and an Absa processing step must both finish before the next rehearsal. The seller's date is uncertain, while Absa's internal lead time is fixed. What is the most useful escalation?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: Escalate the seller date alone, because the external party caused the first delay.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: Ask the cutover manager whether the rehearsal can go ahead, and treat the processing time as an internal planning matter.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Present the full chain of dependencies, the last time the data can arrive, the internal processing limit, the rehearsal consequence, and the decision or recovery options.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: Move the local rehearsal activity to the next available window so the programme forecast reflects the current uncertainty.
  Answer: C
  Feedback: The useful escalation shows the combined dependency and its last workable decision point, not just one party's delay on its own.

title: Relationships
text:
-
  Name: Country leadership and workstreams
  Text: Own local outcomes, activities, stakeholder engagement, evidence and decisions within the authority they have been given. The In-country PMO coordinates and challenges their delivery.
-
  Name: Central Hub
  Text: The Central Hub is the central team that coordinates the overall programme. It owns transaction-wide governance, the single combined plan, links between workstreams, reporting to senior leaders, programme standards and transaction-level escalation. It gives direction and clears Group-wide blockers.
-
  Name: Functional Spokes and control functions
  Text: Functional Spokes are the central specialist teams for each function. They own Group standards, functional design, specialist interpretation and approvals that must stay with them. They give more hands-on delivery support where country skills or authority are limited.
-
  Name: Local external environment
  Text: Includes regulators, customers, employees, suppliers and permitted counterparty contacts. The country supplies the local knowledge and access needed to turn programme assumptions into workable local action.

title: Relevant resources
text:
-
  Name: Local regulatory and commitments tracker
  Text: Tracks local submissions, conditions, evidence, lead times and dependencies through the authorised Compliance and Legal routes.
-
  Name: Testing plan, scripts and evidence
  Text: Records local scenarios, participants, results, defects and acceptance evidence.
-
  Name: Dress-rehearsal defect and checkpoint records
  Text: Track ownership, fixes, seller or Absa dependencies, closure evidence and the maturity expected before the next rehearsal.
-
  Name: Cutover runbook and checkpoint status
  Text: Defines local execution tasks, dependencies, evidence, fallbacks and escalation within the transaction command structure.
-
  Name: Hypercare RAID and local stability status
  Text: Supports fast issue triage, trend visibility, remaining actions and a controlled move to business as usual.

title: Scenarios
text:
-
  Id: s1
  Title: A late legal handover
  Situation: The country PMO joins the transaction after signing. The sale agreement seems to require action on local customer consent before a stated date, but the wording is unfamiliar and the local plan does not yet include this activity. Legal can clarify tomorrow. The customer team needs to reserve outreach capacity this week.
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: Add a customer-consent milestone using the date in the agreement and start detailed planning, subject to later legal confirmation.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: Ask Legal for a plain-language obligation, owner, evidence and deadline. Meanwhile, start reversible capacity and data-preparation actions and record the assumption clearly.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Keep the matter out of the local plan until Legal confirms whether an obligation exists, to avoid an unsupported interpretation in programme controls.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: Escalate the possible obligation to the Central Hub and ask it to decide the local planning treatment before the country commits resources.
  Answer: B
  Feedback: Option B keeps the legal decision with Legal while using the available time for no-regret preparation. Option A risks turning an unverified reading of the agreement into a firm delivery commitment. Option C protects accuracy but loses useful preparation time. Option D makes the uncertainty visible, but it asks the Central Hub to settle a legal and local delivery matter that needs the relevant experts.

title: Scenarios
text:
-
  Id: s2
  Title: Technology green, customer readiness uncertain
  Situation: Four weeks before the readiness gate, the local technology lead reports green. End-to-end configuration is progressing to plan. Customer communications are not yet approved, frontline training dates are provisional and the complaints process has not been tested. No individual milestone is currently late.
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: Keep the local status green, since the committed technology milestones are on plan, and track the customer activities as separate readiness actions.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: Move the whole country status to red, because untested customer and complaints processes are a serious readiness gap.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Build a combined customer-readiness path with owners and evidence, check the forecast against the gate, and report the country position based on the overall operational outcome.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: Ask the Central Hub to set up a Client Readiness workstream before changing the country status or adding new milestones.
  Answer: C
  Feedback: Option C tests the real local outcome instead of letting technology progress stand in for readiness. Option A keeps the technology status accurate but may misstate the country's overall position. Option B may turn out to be right, but it sets the severity before checking whether recovery is still possible. Option D may improve programme structure, but it does not remove the country's job of showing and planning for the local gap now.

title: Scenarios
text:
-
  Id: s3
  Title: A Group blocker in a local plan
  Situation: A local supplier must be onboarded before Legal Day 1 (LD1). The country team has finished its commercial assessment, but Group Procurement must approve an exception to policy. The supplier slot expires in ten working days. The Central Hub asks whether it should take over the supplier action.
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: Hand the activity to the Central Hub, because the remaining decision sits with a Group function and cannot be resolved locally.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: Keep the local supplier outcome with the country, send a complete exception request and impact assessment, and ask the Central Hub to coordinate the Group decision by a set date.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Keep the activity local and ask the supplier to hold the slot while country leadership pursues the exception through normal business channels.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: Add a backup supplier to the local plan and delay Group escalation unless the preferred supplier slot is lost.
  Answer: B
  Feedback: Option B keeps the country's ownership of the delivery outcome while using the Central Hub to clear the Group-level blocker. Option A hands over more ownership than the blocker requires. Option C may use a valid relationship, but it does not protect the deadline through proper programme escalation. Option D gives useful contingency but delays action on the preferred, potentially critical, option.

title: Scenarios
text:
-
  Id: s4
  Title: The same date, different meaning
  Situation: The joint plan states that the seller will provide customer data on 10 May. The seller understands this as an initial extract for review. The country onboarding team assumes it will get a cleansed, approved file it can load straight away. The difference emerges two weeks before the date, with little schedule contingency left.
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: Treat the joint-plan wording as the binding commitment and escalate if the file is not ready to load on 10 May.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: Change the local plan to assume an initial extract, keeping contingency by moving preparation work ahead of receipt.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Agree jointly what will be delivered, in what quality, who approves it, what evidence is needed and the recovery dates, then show the confirmed consequence in both the local and combined plans.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: Ask the Central Hub and counterparty PMO to resolve the disagreement while the country team keeps planning on the load-ready assumption.
  Answer: C
  Feedback: Option C turns an assumed agreement into a hand-off that actually works. Option A relies on wording that both sides read differently. Option B may be sensible for recovery, but it changes the assumption before the parties agree the hand-off. Option D uses the right escalation route but leaves the local plan exposed while others resolve the issue.

title: A defect approaching the next rehearsal
breadcrumb: A defect approaching the next rehearsal
text:
Id: s5
Title: A defect approaching the next rehearsal
Situation: The first dress rehearsal found a data defect jointly owned by Absa and the seller. The seller must approve and send a corrected extract. Absa must then process it through the defect route. Five days before the second rehearsal, approval is still outstanding and Absa's processing takes four days. The cutover manager owns the rehearsal runbook (the timed plan of cutover activities, owners, dependencies and fallback actions).
Options:
  -
    Key: A
    Text: Keep the defect open for the second rehearsal, since the cutover manager can decide whether the affected step stays in scope.
  -
    Key: B
    Text: Ask the seller for an urgent response and prepare to log the same defect again if the corrected data misses the processing window.
  -
    Key: C
    Text: Work out the last time the data can arrive and still be processed, escalate seller approval and Absa processing together, agree how to handle the rehearsal, and record the readiness consequence before the window closes.
  -
    Key: D
    Text: Remove the affected step from the second rehearsal so the rest of the runbook can show progress while the fix continues.
Answer: C

title: A defect approaching the next rehearsal
breadcrumb: A defect approaching the next rehearsal
text: Feedback: Option C manages the whole chain of dependencies rather than treating seller approval and Absa processing as separate problems. Option A recognises the cutover manager's role but delays the readiness decision. Option B may get the data but does not protect the internal processing deadline. Option D may be the right call, but only once the evidence gap and readiness consequence have been assessed through the proper route.

title: Start steps
text:
-
  Title: Get an early deal handover
  Good: The country understands the deal's direction, what is and is not included (the transaction perimeter), its objectives, target dates, affected entities and known findings from due diligence. Open questions and missing information are visible.
  Evidence: Country transaction summary, due diligence handover, key assumptions, information requests and named source owners.
-
  Title: Turn obligations into local actions
  Good: The authorised experts explain legal, regulatory and contractual obligations in plain delivery language. The country understands what must happen, by when, who owns the interpretation and what evidence is needed. The PMO does not interpret legal wording itself.
  Evidence: Plain-language obligation map, source reference, accountable authority, local action, deadline and any open interpretation questions.
-
  Title: Assess country maturity, authority and capacity
  Good: The programme has tested local transaction experience, specialist skills, formally authorised decision-making power, spare capacity, data quality, governance quality and regulatory capability. Gaps have owners and dates for support or backfill.
  Evidence: Country maturity assessment, role appointments, capacity view, business-as-usual constraints, delegated authority and support plan.

title: Start steps
text:
-
  Title: Map the full local impact
  Good: The impact assessment covers customers, employees, operations, products, processes, technology, data, controls, suppliers, property and local legal entities. It does not assume technology is the whole transaction.
  Evidence: Local impact map, customer journeys, stakeholder map, service dependencies, regulatory implications and open design questions.
-
  Title: Agree the central, functional and local split
  Good: Every important activity has one accountable owner and a clear support model. The country owns more where it has the maturity and authority to do so; central and functional teams support more where there is a documented gap.
  Evidence: Country RACI (who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed), execution split, exceptions, decision routes, named deputies and escalation paths.
-
  Title: Build the local delivery controls
  Good: The local plan, RAID log, dependencies, actions, decisions, status and evidence locations follow programme standards while reflecting local activities and lead times. Reporting definitions and deadlines are understood.
  Evidence: Local level-2 plan, controlled logs, governance calendar, status format, evidence index and reporting cut-offs.

title: Start steps
text:
-
  Title: Check that hand-offs mean the same thing to both sides
  Good: For each central, functional or counterparty hand-off, both sides agree the content, format, acceptance criteria (the conditions that must be met before it is accepted), owner, due date and evidence of completion. A date in a joint plan is not treated as proof that both sides agree.
  Evidence: Interface directory, hand-off definitions, acceptance criteria, joint assumptions, dependency owners and escalation dates.
-
  Title: Plan readiness and transition early
  Good: Testing, dress rehearsals (practice runs of the cutover plan), cutover, customer and employee readiness, contingency, hypercare and business-as-usual handover are planned before execution pressure makes them hard to add.
  Evidence: Readiness criteria, test and rehearsal implications, cutover ownership, fallback assumptions, hypercare model and BAU acceptance route.

title: Success measures
text:
-
  - Early local involvement
  - local implications are visible before mobilisation plans are fixed.
-
  - Local plan quality
  - country activities, owners, resources, dependencies and evidence can actually be delivered.
-
  - Ownership clarity
  - central, functional and local responsibilities are clear and agreed.
-
  - Customer and operational readiness
  - technology progress is connected to real customer journeys and local operations.
-
  - Issue resolution
  - local matters are solved quickly, and Group blockers are escalated with the full facts.
-
  - Interface reliability
  - central, country and counterparty hand-offs mean the same thing to everyone involved.
-
  - Evidence quality
  - status and readiness are backed by controlled local evidence.
-
  - Local value protection
  - customer, cost, timing, supplier and business-case impacts are raised early.

title: Four days to the readiness decision
breadcrumb: Workstream Lead pathway — modules and exercises
Four days to the readiness decision
text:
Title: Four days to the readiness decision
Intro: Your workstream is approaching its readiness recommendation:
Facts:
  - required configuration is complete, but the evidence pack has not been accepted by the control owner;
  - a dependent workstream expects to deliver an interface one day late, within the current schedule buffer, but no joint recovery trigger is agreed;
  - a supplier proposes an additional requirement that may improve stability but adds cost and one week if adopted now; and
  - the fallback procedure passed a desktop review but has not been rehearsed with the people who would operate it.
Close: The Workstream Executive believes the overall position can remain green if the open items are converted into conditions. The programme needs your recommendation today.
Improved: You are now applying the Workstream Lead role through mandate, evidence and programme impact, not activity alone.
Review: You have completed the pathway. Review the highlighted module before using the playbook in a live workstream decision.

title: Capstone decisions
breadcrumb: Workstream Lead pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: plan
  Question: How should completion and status be represented?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Report configuration as complete and green, and track control-owner acceptance as a time-bound follow-up action.
      Feedback: Acceptance is part of completion, not a follow-up. This overstates the milestone.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Separate built configuration from unaccepted evidence, and report the forecast against the agreed criteria with the owner and date for acceptance.
      Feedback: Recommended. It protects the acceptance criteria and gives a usable forecast.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Report red until the control owner accepts the evidence pack, and pause all related preparation work.
      Feedback: Transparent, but a bigger response than needed while safe work can continue.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Move acceptance into a later milestone so configuration can be closed, subject to baseline approval.
      Feedback: Only valid if governance genuinely approves the change, not to quietly close the milestone.
  Answer: b
  Reasoning: The agreed milestone includes acceptance. Report what is done, what is not yet accepted, and what the forecast depends on.

title: Capstone decisions
breadcrumb: Workstream Lead pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: dependencies
  Question: How should the dependency and schedule buffer be controlled?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Accept the one-day slip because it sits within the buffer, and review again if the date moves further.
      Feedback: The buffer absorbs it, but without a trigger nobody knows when to act.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Ask the PMO to manage the interface date in the integrated plan while your team protects its own milestones.
      Feedback: Recognises the PMO role but hands away ownership of the dependency.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Agree with the other Workstream Lead a recovery trigger, a decision point and hand-off criteria, and record them in the dependency log.
      Feedback: Recommended. It turns a verbal forecast into a controlled, jointly owned hand-off.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Rebaseline your plan to the later date now, so the buffer is preserved for other risks.
      Feedback: Cautious, but it rebaselines before recovery options have been tested.
  Answer: c
  Reasoning: Hand-offs between teams must be explicit, agreed and tracked, with a clear point at which the buffer is no longer enough.

title: Capstone decisions
breadcrumb: Workstream Lead pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: mandate
  Question: What should happen to the supplier's additional requirement?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Adopt it now using workstream contingency, because stability matters more than one week, and record it in RAID.
      Feedback: Treats delegated tolerance as permission to change scope and timing.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Quantify the cost, timing and stability effects, and take a recommendation to the authority that owns the scope and date.
      Feedback: Recommended. The choice changes timing and cost, so it needs the right authority.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Reject it for now to protect the date, and ask the supplier to raise it again during hypercare.
      Feedback: Protects the date but makes a trade-off that is not yours to make alone.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Ask the supplier to start preliminary design under the existing contract while the decision is considered.
      Feedback: Creates commercial momentum before the decision basis is understood.
  Answer: b
  Reasoning: A change to cost and timing is outside the Workstream Lead's mandate. Frame it as a decision with options and a recommendation.

title: Capstone decisions
breadcrumb: Workstream Lead pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: readiness
  Question: What readiness recommendation should be made, and what must be escalated?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Recommend green with conditions, as the Workstream Executive suggests, and track the open items through hypercare.
      Feedback: Converts unproven items into conditions without checking whether the evidence is enough.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Recommend not ready until every item is fully closed, regardless of the agreed readiness criteria.
      Feedback: May be right in the end, but skips the test of proportionality against the criteria.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Give a conditional recommendation based on the controls the operators have agreed to run, leaving the fallback as it is.
      Feedback: Relies on acceptance alone. The fallback has not been proven with the operators.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Compare evidence with the criteria, state what is unproven, including the fallback rehearsal, and escalate remaining risk for acceptance by the right authority.
      Feedback: Recommended. It gives an honest, evidence-based recommendation without taking the decision for others.
  Answer: d
  Reasoning: Readiness is an evidence-based recommendation. Unproven fallbacks and remaining risk must be made explicit and accepted by the correct authority.

title: Decision sequence
breadcrumb: Workstream Lead pathway — modules and exercises
text:
- Confirm the facts and evidence.
- Identify the effect on scope, timing, cost, value, control and other workstreams.
- Determine who has authority.
- Develop credible options and a recommendation.
- State the final useful decision date.
- Record and implement the outcome.

title: Four weeks to integrated testing
breadcrumb: Workstream Lead pathway — modules and exercises
text:
Title: Four weeks to integrated testing
Intro: Your workstream is reporting green. Four weeks before integrated testing:
Facts:
  - a key control design is drafted but the control owner has not accepted it;
  - the specialist named in the plan can provide two days a week rather than the four assumed;
  - another workstream has verbally agreed a data hand-off date, but the hand-off content and acceptance standard are not recorded; and
  - the team believes the lost time can be recovered during testing.
Close: The weekly status is due today. The Workstream Executive and Programme Manager both expect a clear recommendation.
Message: Several choices can look reasonable in isolation. The rest of the pathway shows how mandate, evidence and programme impact determine the best response.

title: Diagnostic decisions
breadcrumb: Workstream Lead pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: mandate
  Question: The specialist can give only half the time assumed. What is your first move?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Work out the minimum specialist input needed, compare resequencing with backfill, and take a recommended response to the Workstream Executive.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Ask the functional head to restore the full allocation, and have the Workstream PM model the plan impact if they decline.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Ask the Workstream PM to resequence the review work and decide the new order, then record the capacity gap as a risk.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Pass the capacity gap to the Central Hub, because specialist availability can affect the integrated programme plan.
  Answer: a
-
  Capability: plan
  Question: How should today's status represent the workstream?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Keep green, because the team expects to recover the time during testing, and note the open items in the narrative.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Report the forecast against the testing date, showing the unaccepted control design, reduced capacity and recovery assumption with owners.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Move to red, because the control design and specialist capacity both fall short of the approved plan today.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Report green for completed activity and amber for the remaining work, so both views are visible to the programme.
  Answer: b

title: Diagnostic decisions
breadcrumb: Workstream Lead pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: dependencies
  Question: What should happen with the verbally agreed data hand-off?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Rely on the verbal date for now, and confirm the content once the supplying workstream has started the extract.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Ask the PMO to record the date in the integrated plan, while your team plans against the verbal agreement.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Agree the hand-off content, acceptance standard, date and owner with the other Workstream Lead, and record it in the dependency log.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Add a buffer to your own plan to allow for the hand-off being late, without reopening the conversation.
  Answer: c
-
  Capability: readiness
  Question: What must be true before you can make a credible readiness claim for testing?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: The team is confident it can recover the lost time, and the Workstream Executive supports the plan.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: The control design is accepted, the hand-off is agreed and evidenced, and capacity supports the forecast, or gaps are escalated.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: The control design has been drafted and shared, with acceptance tracked as a follow-up action.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: All open items are logged in RAID with owners, even if acceptance is still outstanding when testing starts.
  Answer: b

title: Escalation missing
breadcrumb: Workstream Lead pathway — modules and exercises

  Feedback: Recommended. Without the authority and a deadline, the options cannot become a decision in time.

Options are to add a weekend validation cycle at an estimated cost of R350,000 or move the test start by two days. The workstream recommends the weekend cycle. A programme decision is required by Wednesday.

title: Boundary
text: the integrated programme plan, the transaction business case, formal go or no-go authority (the formal decision on whether the transaction is ready and safe to proceed), reserved approvals (decisions that must remain with a named senior, central or specialist authority), or legal transaction decisions. You do own the quality and timeliness of the functional input that feeds those decisions.

title: Economics
Glossary
text:
-
  Term: RAID
  Def: Risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies — the log used to track and manage them.
-
  Term: Acceptance criteria
  Def: The conditions that must be met before an output is accepted as complete.
-
  Term: Readiness evidence
  Def: Proof that the required people, processes, technology, data and controls are ready.
-
  Term: Residual risk
  Def: Risk that remains after the agreed controls or actions have been applied.
-
  Term: Dependency
  Def: An input, decision or activity that another task relies on.
-
  Term: Critical path
  Def: The activities and dependencies that directly determine the delivery date.
-
  Term: Delegated authority
  Def: The decisions a role has been formally authorised to make.
-
  Term: Reserved decision
  Def: A decision that must remain with a named senior, central or specialist authority.
-
  Term: Baseline
  Def: The approved plan, budget or scope against which progress is measured.
-
  Term: Rebaseline
  Def: To formally approve a change to that plan, budget or scope.
-
  Term: Cutover
  Def: The controlled move from the current state to the new operating state.
-
  Term: Runbook
  Def: The timed plan of cutover activities, owners, dependencies and fallback actions.
-
  Term: Dress rehearsal
  Def: A practice run of the cutover plan before live execution.
-
  Term: Go or no-go
  Def: The formal decision on whether the transaction is ready and safe to proceed.
-
  Term: Hypercare
  Def: The period of increased monitoring and support immediately after cutover.

title: Glossary
text:
-
  Term: Business as usual (BAU)
  Def: When ongoing ownership returns to normal teams.
-
  Term: Transaction perimeter
  Def: What is and is not included in the deal.
-
  Term: Integrated programme plan
  Def: The single programme plan that combines all workstreams and key dates.
-
  Term: Escalation
  Def: Raising a matter to someone with the authority or support needed to resolve it.
-
  Term: Decision rights
  Def: Who can make which decisions.

title: Mobilise steps
text:
-
  Title: Accept the role and confirm your authority
  Good: You understand the expected outcomes, decision rights (who can make which decisions), escalation route and time commitment. You have accepted the role, and you have named a deputy where continuity is needed.
  Evidence: Confirmed appointment, decision mandate, named deputy and agreed availability.
-
  Title: Understand the transaction context
  Good: You understand the transaction objectives, the transaction perimeter (what is and is not included in the deal), target dates, known diligence findings, legal or information restrictions, key commitments and what these mean for your function.
  Evidence: Documented assumptions, constraints, known commitments and questions that need clarifying.
-
  Title: Confirm capacity and capability
  Good: You have identified the required specialists. You have checked existing business-as-usual deadlines, leave, regulatory commitments and other change work. Gaps have an agreed response, such as reprioritising, backfill or specialist support.
  Evidence: Resource view, capacity constraints, required skills, named owners and agreed actions to close gaps.
-
  Title: Set up interfaces
  Good: The split between central, functional and regional execution is clear. You have named interfaces with other workstreams and any permitted counterparty contacts. The team knows where hand-offs and joint decisions will happen.
  Evidence: Interface directory, dependency owners and an agreed way of working together.

title: Mobilise steps
text:
-
  Title: Set up delivery controls
  Good: The team can access the controlled programme workspace and current governance, planning, reporting, RAID (risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies) and decision-log templates. Owners know how and when to maintain these controls.
  Evidence: Access confirmed, meeting cadence set, controls assigned and reporting dates understood.
-
  Title: Brief the team
  Good: The team understands the objectives, restrictions, roles, decision rights, planning window and immediate actions. You record questions and open assumptions rather than leaving them unspoken.
  Evidence: Briefing attendance, role acknowledgement, actions, open questions and escalation items.
-
  Title: Prepare for the planning work after the gate
  Good: You have the right people and source information ready to define the workstream charter, process brick, blueprint, detailed plan, resources, dependencies, costs and acceptance criteria once the mobilisation gate is passed.
  Evidence: Workshop plan, participants, inputs, initial scope ideas and priority questions.

title: Playbook
text:
-
  Title: Before accepting a plan
  Items:
    - Is the scope clear and linked to a defined outcome?
    - Are activities, owners and dates detailed enough to execute?
    - Have you tested resource capacity and specialist skills?
    - Are all significant dependencies and hand-offs explicit?
    - Are acceptance criteria and evidence requirements defined?
    - Do costs, benefits and key assumptions match the value case?
-
  Title: Before each workstream session
  Items:
    - Is the detailed plan up to date?
    - Is evidence backing up the milestone forecasts?
    - Have risks, issues, assumptions or dependencies changed?
    - Which decisions are needed, from whom and by when?
    - What must you escalate to the Transaction Working Group?
    - Is there any cost or readiness impact that is not yet visible?
-
  Title: Before reporting green
  Items:
    - Have you achieved the outcome, not just completed the activity?
    - Has the required evidence been produced and accepted?
    - Are downstream owners ready to receive the output?
    - Are residual risks understood and owned?
    - Is the forecast credible given current capacity and dependencies?

title: Playbook
text:
-
  Title: Before a readiness recommendation
  Items:
    - Are people, process, technology, data, controls and operations ready?
    - Have you completed the required tests and rehearsals?
    - Are defects and remaining actions understood?
    - Are runbook tasks, checkpoints, fallbacks and communications ready to execute?
    - Are conditions, exceptions and residual risks explicit?
    - Can formal decision-makers see the evidence behind your recommendation?

title: Principles
text:
- Own the outcome, not just the activity.
- Make the detailed plan executable.
- Treat capacity as a delivery fact, not an assumption.
- Make dependencies visible before they fail.
- Bring choices and consequences to decision-makers.
- Report forecast and evidence honestly.
- Escalate before the date is missed.
- Define readiness in terms of accepted evidence.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: The Workstream PM finds that two activities need the same scarce specialist. Both stay within agreed scope, and either order can still meet the programme milestone. The Workstream PM prepares a preferred sequence. What should happen next?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: The Workstream PM confirms the sequence, because maintaining the detailed plan sits within the project-management role, then tells the Workstream Lead.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: The Workstream Lead makes the prioritisation decision using the impact analysis, and the Workstream PM records the decision and updates the plan and controls.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: The Workstream Executive decides, because any competition for specialist capacity is a workstream trade-off.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: The PMO decides, because using a scarce resource could affect confidence in the integrated programme plan.
  Answer: B
  Feedback: Option B is the recommended response. Why: the Workstream PM should provide analysis and planning discipline, but prioritising within agreed workstream scope stays with the Workstream Lead. Trade-off: Executive or PMO involvement is only needed where the choice goes beyond that mandate or affects wider programme outcomes.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: A lower-priority workstream activity can move by one week to free up internal capacity for a critical milestone. This does not change programme scope, budget, acceptance criteria or any cross-workstream date. What should the Workstream Lead do?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: Make the reprioritisation within the workstream, record the reason and update the plan, while checking that the stated programme impacts stay unchanged.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: Seek Workstream Executive approval, because any change to the approved workstream baseline is a trade-off decision.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Ask the Workstream PM to approve the change, because it concerns sequencing rather than functional scope.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: Submit the change to the PMO for approval before updating the detailed plan, even though no integrated milestone changes.
  Answer: A
  Feedback: Option A is the recommended response. Why: the Workstream Lead can prioritise resources and activities beneath agreed programme milestones. Trade-off: the change should stay controlled and visible, but it does not need to move to another decision-maker when the stated conditions genuinely hold.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: Your team has completed and internally approved an output. The receiving workstream has not confirmed that the hand-off meets its agreed acceptance criteria by the reporting cut-off. The supplier expects no schedule impact if acceptance arrives within two days. The milestone definition includes accepted hand-off. How should this be reported?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: Red, because part of the milestone criteria was not met at the reporting cut-off, regardless of the current forecast.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: Green with a narrative note, because the producing workstream has completed its activity and no delay is currently forecast.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Complete in the workstream plan, with the receiving workstream's acceptance tracked separately as a dependency.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: Qualify the status to show the milestone is not yet accepted, state the owner and two-day decision point, and show the forecast impact if acceptance is not secured.
  Answer: D
  Feedback: Option D is the recommended response. Why: the agreed milestone includes acceptance, so completing the internal work alone is not enough. Trade-off: the response should separate current completion from forecast impact, without treating every evidence gap as an automatic critical failure.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: A supplier says an emerging requirement may cost between R800,000 and R1.4 million. The requirement is still being checked, but a decision is needed within five business days to protect the delivery date. What is the best response?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: Wait for a firm requirement and fixed estimate, so governance gets one reliable number rather than a provisional range.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: Use the upper end of the range in the forecast, as this is the most cautious basis until the requirement is confirmed.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Present the range, assumptions, delivery and value implications, available options and decision deadline through the agreed Finance and change-control route.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: Keep the item in workstream RAID until the requirement is confirmed, then raise a change request if the agreed budget is exceeded.
  Answer: C
  Feedback: Option C is the recommended response. Why: a decision can be supported by a reasoned range when the uncertainty is stated clearly. Trade-off: waiting for precision may remove the programme's ability to act in time, and using only the upper estimate hides the assumptions and choices behind it.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: All mandatory tests have passed, but the final test used an agreed temporary workaround. The workaround has a named owner, a 30-day expiry date and monitoring controls. The readiness criteria allow temporary controls that are accepted in this way. How should the Workstream Lead frame the recommendation?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: Recommend not ready, because a workaround means the target operating state has not been fully reached.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: Give a conditional readiness recommendation that states the supporting evidence, residual risk, monitoring, accountable owner and exit date.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Recommend ready without qualification, because the criteria explicitly allow temporary controls and all tests passed.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: Give the facts to the PMO without a recommendation, because formal readiness decisions sit outside the Workstream Lead's authority.
  Answer: B
  Feedback: Option B is the recommended response. Why: the Workstream Lead should give a clear recommendation even though the formal decision sits elsewhere. Trade-off: the temporary control may well support readiness, but its conditions and residual risk must stay visible to the decision-maker.

title: Roles
text:
-
  Id: lead
  Name: Workstream Lead
  Text: You own delivery for your function: the detailed plan, functional decisions within your mandate, readiness evidence and the workstream's status.
-
  Id: pm
  Name: Workstream PM
  Text: The Workstream PM keeps the detailed plan and governance on track, maintains delivery controls, and prepares you to report. The Workstream PM does not make your decisions and does not carry your accountability.
-
  Id: exec
  Name: Workstream Executive
  Text: The Workstream Executive is accountable for the workstream outcome, removes blockers, approves major workstream trade-offs, and signs off decisions or deliverables that need executive authority.
-
  Id: hub
  Name: Central Hub and PMO
  Text: The Central Hub is the central Inorganic Change team that coordinates the overall programme, including the single programme plan that combines all workstreams (the integrated programme plan), governance, standards, quality checks, cross-workstream coordination and reporting to senior leaders. It does not own your function's delivery.

title: Capacity against a fixed date
text:
Title: Capacity against a fixed date
Situation: The approved plan assumes a control specialist supports the workstream for two days a week over the next month. Their line manager can currently release them for only half a day a week. The plan has three days of float (spare time before this affects the delivery date). The Workstream PM thinks some review work could be resequenced. The next status report is due tomorrow.
Options:
  -
    Key: A
    Text: Use the available float to resequence the review, record the capacity gap as a risk, and reconsider escalating after the first week of delivery.
  -
    Key: B
    Text: Ask the functional head to restore the assumed allocation, while the Workstream PM models the likely change to plan and budget if the request is declined.
  -
    Key: C
    Text: Check the minimum specialist input actually needed, compare resequencing against backfill, and take a recommended response to the Workstream Executive and PMO before the float runs out.
  -
    Key: D
    Text: Move the status to amber, request extra resource, and keep the current sequence while you clarify the specialist requirement at the next workstream session.
Answer: C

title: Capacity against a fixed date
text: Feedback: Option C combines delivery ownership with proportionate escalation. It best fits your authority: first work out what input you genuinely need, then show the forecast impact and realistic recovery choices to the right people. The trade-off in the other options: A uses float but delays visibility of a planning assumption that no longer holds; B seeks the preferred resource outcome without testing alternatives or showing the wider impact; D makes the risk visible but does not yet give a decision-ready response.

title: Completion and acceptance
text:
Title: Completion and acceptance
Situation: A target process design is complete and the process owner has signed it off. The agreed milestone criteria also require the control owner to accept it. The control owner has reviewed it verbally with no objection, but written evidence will only be available next week. A downstream technology team wants to start configuration now, though no irreversible build work is due for four days.
Options:
  -
    Key: A
    Text: Report the milestone as green with a condition, allow configuration to begin, and track written acceptance as a time-bound action before any irreversible build work.
  -
    Key: B
    Text: Separate accepted design from outstanding control acceptance, allow agreed reversible preparation, and report status against the forecast for meeting the existing exit criteria.
  -
    Key: C
    Text: Report the milestone as amber and pause downstream activity until written acceptance is recorded, keeping the agreed control and hand-off sequence.
  -
    Key: D
    Text: Move control acceptance into a later milestone, subject to normal baseline approval, so design completion and downstream preparation can be reported separately.
Answer: B

title: Completion and acceptance
text: Feedback: Option B protects the agreed acceptance criteria without stopping work that can safely continue. The trade-off in the other options: A risks overstating the milestone, because the condition is part of completion, not just a follow-up item; C is transparent but may be a bigger response than needed; D may only be valid if governance genuinely approves a new way of measuring the milestone, rather than being used to quietly close the original one.

title: A contested dependency date
text:
Title: A contested dependency date
Situation: Testing in your workstream depends on a data extract from another workstream. Its latest working date is four days later than the date in your plan, though its lead believes recovery is possible. Your team can absorb two days by resequencing; any further delay would compress testing. Neither date is yet confirmed in the integrated programme plan.
Options:
  -
    Key: A
    Text: Check the date, hand-off criteria and recovery actions jointly with the other workstream, use the two-day mitigation, and show the remaining testing impact through the integrated dependency process.
  -
    Key: B
    Text: Keep the date already in your plan until the supplying workstream formally changes its forecast, while recording the later date and testing compression as risks.
  -
    Key: C
    Text: Adopt the later date and submit a rebaseline (formally approve a change to the plan, budget or scope) so your workstream plan reflects the more cautious information while recovery continues.
  -
    Key: D
    Text: Ask the PMO to reconcile the dates in the integrated plan while your team protects its own milestones and plans against the original assumption.
Answer: A
Feedback: Option A actively manages both the hand-off and the effect on your own plan. The trade-off in the other options: B keeps a planning assumption that is no longer supported; C is cautious but rebaselines before recovery and hand-off options have been tested; D recognises the PMO's coordination role but hands too much ownership of the dependency away from the Workstream Lead.

title: An emerging requirement
text:
Title: An emerging requirement
Situation: A late regulatory interpretation may require extra validation before go-live. Legal has not yet confirmed whether it is mandatory. A supplier estimates the change could cost between R2 million and R4 million and add one to two weeks, depending on the final interpretation. Some analysis can start without committing to the build.
Options:
  -
    Key: A
    Text: Ask the supplier to reserve delivery capacity and start preliminary design under the existing arrangement, because the requirement may become mandatory and delay could cost more than early mobilisation.
  -
    Key: B
    Text: Time-box the no-regret analysis, quantify the credible cost and timing outcomes, and seek a decision through the agreed authority before making any irreversible commitment.
  -
    Key: C
    Text: Pause related activity until Legal confirms the requirement, while protecting the approved baseline (the approved plan, budget or scope used to measure progress) and supplier commitment date through the risk process.
  -
    Key: D
    Text: Use available workstream contingency for initial delivery, record the uncertainty in RAID, and submit formal change control if the final requirement exceeds delegated tolerance.
Answer: B

title: An emerging requirement
text: Feedback: Option B keeps momentum while protecting decision authority and being open about the cost picture. The trade-off in the other options: A may create commercial momentum before the decision basis is understood; C protects the baseline but may waste time that could be used for reversible analysis; D treats delegated budget tolerance as permission to change scope and does not fully address the wider programme impact.

title: Readiness with a qualified fallback
text:
Title: Readiness with a qualified fallback
Situation: The dress rehearsal (a practice run of the cutover plan before live execution) has passed its core sequence. A fallback procedure worked in an earlier rehearsal using a lower transaction volume. One open issue has low likelihood but high impact if it occurs. A backup manual procedure has been tested in a tabletop exercise, but not at full volume. The readiness criteria allow temporary controls where the residual risk is made explicit.
Options:
  -
    Key: A
    Text: Recommend ready because the core sequence passed and the fallback has prior evidence, with the open issue managed through closer monitoring during hypercare (the period of increased monitoring and support immediately after cutover).
  -
    Key: B
    Text: Compare the available evidence against the agreed criteria, state the residual risk and evidence limits, set conditions and monitoring, and give a clear recommendation.
  -
    Key: C
    Text: Recommend not ready until the fallback and manual procedure have both been repeated at full volume, given the possible impact.
  -
    Key: D
    Text: Recommend conditionally ready if the accountable owners accept the manual procedure and closer monitoring, using the current risk assessment as the basis for approval.
Answer: B

title: Readiness with a qualified fallback
text: Feedback: Option B gives decision-makers an evidence-based recommendation without taking their decision for them. The trade-off in the other options: A may understate the effect of the higher live volume; C may ultimately be right, but it reaches that view without first testing proportionality against the agreed criteria; D recognises the need for conditions but relies on acceptance alone rather than checking whether the evidence is sufficient.

title: Status content
Success measures
text:
-
  - Delivery against plan
  - you achieve outcomes and milestones, or you accurately reforecast them.
-
  - Plan quality
  - activities, resources, dependencies and acceptance criteria are complete and credible.
-
  - Functional readiness
  - people, process, technology, controls and operations are ready for the change.
-
  - Risk control
  - significant risks and issues have owners, actions, dates and clear escalation routes.
-
  - Dependency management
  - hand-offs between teams are explicit, agreed and tracked.
-
  - Decision effectiveness
  - decisions are framed early, taken at the right level and recorded.
-
  - Reporting discipline
  - status reports are short, evidence-based and focused on exceptions.
-
  - Cutover preparedness
  - tasks, fallbacks, checkpoints and owners are ready to execute.

title: Weekly rhythm
text:
-
  Title: Refresh the delivery picture
  Text: Update the detailed plan, milestone forecast, RAID, dependencies, decisions and actions. Check that the plan reflects the work still needed, not just the activity already recorded.
-
  Title: Check with owners
  Text: Test progress, evidence, resource capacity and hand-offs with the people doing the work. Resolve issues within the workstream wherever your mandate allows.
-
  Title: Run the workstream session
  Text: The Workstream Executive chairs the weekly workstream session and the Workstream Lead runs it. Use the detailed plan and workstream RAID as the main inputs. Agree status, key risks, dependencies, decisions and matters to escalate.
-
  Title: Publish the status
  Text: Issue a short workstream status report based on forecast and evidence. State what has changed, what is at risk, what decision is needed, who owns the response and by when.
-
  Title: Connect into the programme
  Text: Represent the workstream at the Transaction Working Group and other relevant forums. Confirm dependencies with other workstreams, raise exceptions, and bring programme decisions back to your team.
-
  Title: Act between meetings
  Text: Do not save serious issues for a meeting. Escalate urgent blockers straight away, record the outcome, and update the plan and controls.

title: Three days to the workstream readiness review
breadcrumb: Workstream Project Manager pathway — modules and exercises
Three days to the workstream readiness review
text:
Title: Three days to the workstream readiness review
Intro: Your workstream is preparing for its readiness review:
Facts:
  - the output is built, but the approver has not accepted the evidence;
  - a dependent interface is forecast one day late, within schedule buffer, but no recovery trigger is recorded;
  - a supplier request could improve stability, but adds cost and requires a scope decision; and
  - the cutover owner says the fallback is understood, although the operating team has not rehearsed it.
Close: The Workstream Lead needs your view to prepare the readiness recommendation.
Improved: You are now applying the Project Manager role through reliable controls, evidence and clear boundaries.
Review: You have completed the pathway. Review the highlighted module before using the playbook on a live workstream.

title: Capstone decisions
breadcrumb: Workstream Project Manager pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: plan
  Question: How should completion and status be recorded?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Record the output as complete and track evidence acceptance as a follow-up action with a date.
      Feedback: Acceptance is part of completion. This overstates the milestone.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Show the output as built but not complete against its acceptance criteria, with the approver and forecast date.
      Feedback: Recommended. It keeps completion tied to the agreed condition and gives a usable forecast.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Move acceptance into a later milestone so the build milestone can close on time.
      Feedback: Only valid through approved change control, not to close a milestone quietly.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Report the output as red and pause related readiness work until the approver responds.
      Feedback: Visible, but a bigger response than needed while safe work can continue.
  Answer: b
  Reasoning: The plan defines completion by acceptance and evidence, not by production alone.

title: Capstone decisions
breadcrumb: Workstream Project Manager pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: control
  Question: How should the late interface be controlled?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Accept the slip because it is within buffer, and review it again if the date moves further.
      Feedback: The buffer absorbs it today, but without a trigger nobody knows when to act.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Rebaseline the plan to the later date now so the buffer is kept for other risks.
      Feedback: Changes the baseline before recovery options are tested or approved.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Agree a recovery trigger, decision point and hand-off criteria with the supplying team, and record them in the dependency log.
      Feedback: Recommended. It turns a forecast into a controlled, jointly owned hand-off.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Ask the Central PMO to manage the interface date while you protect your own milestones.
      Feedback: Recognises the programme view but hands away control of the dependency.
  Answer: c
  Reasoning: A dependency is controlled when both sides agree what is delivered, when, and at what point the buffer is no longer enough.

title: Capstone decisions
breadcrumb: Workstream Project Manager pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: mandate
  Question: How should the supplier request enter the decision process?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Add it to the plan as a provisional activity so its delivery effect stays visible while it is discussed.
      Feedback: Changes the plan before anyone with authority has decided.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Record it as a proposed change, assess its cost, timing, scope and stability effects, and route it to the approving authority.
      Feedback: Recommended. You control the assessment and record; the authorised owner decides.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Decline it for now to protect the review date, and ask the supplier to raise it in hypercare.
      Feedback: Makes a scope trade-off that is not the Project Manager's to make.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Ask the supplier to start preliminary work at risk so the time is not lost.
      Feedback: Creates cost and scope exposure before authority is confirmed.
  Answer: b
  Reasoning: Useful changes are not automatically approved. The baseline holds until the right owner decides.

title: Capstone decisions
breadcrumb: Workstream Project Manager pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: status
  Question: What readiness information should you give the Workstream Lead?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: A recommendation of ready with conditions, since the cutover owner is confident in the fallback.
      Feedback: Makes the recommendation for the Lead and relies on confidence rather than proof.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: A list of open actions, so the Lead can decide which to convert into conditions.
      Feedback: Useful, but without evidence status and decisions it does not support a recommendation.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: A request to delay the review until every item is closed, to avoid a conditional result.
      Feedback: Pre-empts a decision that belongs to the Lead and governance.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: An evidence view showing what is accepted, what is unproven, including the unrehearsed fallback, and the decisions needed.
      Feedback: Recommended. It gives the Lead a reliable basis for their recommendation.
  Answer: d
  Reasoning: The Project Manager maintains the evidence and control view. The Workstream Lead owns the readiness recommendation.

title: Control options
breadcrumb: Workstream Project Manager pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Id: a
  Text: Update the plan now, because the Lead owns workstream priorities, and add the reason at the next meeting.
  Feedback: The change is within the Lead's authority, but the plan moves before the decision is traceable.
-
  Id: b
  Text: Confirm the decision and affected owners with the Lead, record it in the decision log, then update the plan and actions.
  Feedback: Recommended. It respects the Lead's authority and keeps a traceable record before the plan changes.
-
  Id: c
  Text: Raise a change request to the Workstream Executive, because an activity has moved from the baseline.
  Feedback: Scope and programme dates are unchanged, so this is within the Lead's authority, not a baseline change.
-
  Id: d
  Text: Hold the plan until the Central PMO confirms the integrated programme is unaffected.
  Feedback: The Central PMO does not own workstream priorities. Waiting leaves the record wrong.

title: Control types
breadcrumb: Workstream Project Manager pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Title: Risk
  Text: Something that may happen and would affect delivery.
-
  Title: Assumption
  Text: Something treated as true for planning that has not been confirmed.
-
  Title: Issue
  Text: Something that has happened and is affecting delivery now.
-
  Title: Dependency
  Text: An input, decision or activity that another task relies on.
-
  Title: Action
  Text: A task with an owner and date to resolve something.
-
  Title: Decision
  Text: A choice made by the right owner, recorded with its reason and date.

title: Cycle
breadcrumb: Workstream Project Manager pathway — modules and exercises

  Title: Refresh facts

-

title: Five weeks to integrated testing
breadcrumb: Workstream Project Manager pathway — modules and exercises
text:
Title: Five weeks to integrated testing
Intro: The detailed workstream plan shows most activities as on track, but:
Facts:
  - several outputs have dates but no recorded acceptance standard;
  - a supplier has proposed a change that the team has started assessing, but it is not in the change record;
  - a dependency on another workstream is supported by a verbal agreement only; and
  - the Workstream Lead wants to retain green status while the team works through the gaps.
Close: The weekly status report is due tomorrow.
Message: Several choices can look reasonable in isolation. The modules show how the Project Manager's controls, evidence and boundaries decide the best response.

title: Diagnostic decisions
breadcrumb: Workstream Project Manager pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: mandate
  Question: The Workstream Lead wants to keep green. Where does your role start and stop?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Set the status yourself using the reporting definitions, because you produce the status report.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Accept the Lead's view, because the Workstream Lead owns status and is accountable for recovery.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Show the Lead the gaps, evidence and forecast effect, and ask them to confirm status against the definitions.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Report green to the Lead and flag the gaps separately to the Central PMO as a programme risk.
  Answer: c
-
  Capability: plan
  Question: What would make the plan executable rather than just dated?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Add a percentage-complete column so owners can show progress each week against each date.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Agree acceptance criteria, owners and evidence for each output, and link them to the dependent dates.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Break every activity into smaller tasks so each one can be tracked daily by the team.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Add contingency to each date so outputs can be accepted later without moving the plan.
  Answer: b

title: Diagnostic decisions
breadcrumb: Workstream Project Manager pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Capability: control
  Question: How should the verbal dependency and the supplier's proposed change be handled?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Record the dependency with both owners and acceptance terms, and log the proposed change for assessment and approval.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Leave both as they are until the team finishes assessing the change, then update all records together.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Add the supplier change to the plan now so its timing is visible, and confirm the dependency next week.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: Ask the Central PMO to own the dependency and the supplier change, as both affect other teams.
  Answer: a
-
  Capability: status
  Question: What status and escalation should you prepare?
  Options:
    -
      Id: a
      Text: Green with a commentary noting the open gaps, as the Lead expects to close them this week.
    -
      Id: b
      Text: Red, because acceptance standards, the change record and the dependency are all incomplete.
    -
      Id: c
      Text: Amber, set by you, with the Lead able to override the rating if they disagree.
    -
      Id: d
      Text: A forecast against the testing date showing each gap, its owner and the decision needed, for the Lead to confirm.
  Answer: d

title: Plan parts
breadcrumb: Workstream Project Manager pathway — modules and exercises
text:
-
  Title: Outcome
  Text: What the activity must achieve, not just produce.
-
  Title: Owner
  Text: One named person accountable for completing it.
-
  Title: Sequence and dates

-

title: Economics
Glossary
text:
-
  Term: Scope
  Def: The work and outcomes included in the workstream.
-
  Term: Detailed workstream plan (L2 plan)
  Def: The plan showing activities, owners, dates, dependencies and completion conditions.
-
  Term: Acceptance criteria
  Def: The conditions that must be met before an output is accepted as complete.
-
  Term: Dependency
  Def: An input, decision or activity that another task relies on.
-
  Term: RAID
  Def: Risks, assumptions, issues and dependencies.
-
  Term: RAG status
  Def: Red, amber or green status.
-
  Term: Baseline
  Def: The approved scope, plan or budget used to measure progress.
-
  Term: Change control
  Def: The agreed process for assessing and approving a change to that baseline.
-
  Term: Critical path
  Def: The activities and dependencies that directly determine the overall delivery date.
-
  Term: Readiness evidence
  Def: Proof that the required people, processes, technology, data and controls are ready.
-
  Term: Residual risk
  Def: Risk that remains after the agreed actions or controls have been applied.
-
  Term: Escalation
  Def: Raising a matter to someone with the authority or support needed to resolve it.
-
  Term: Dress rehearsal
  Def: A practice run before live execution.
-
  Term: Cutover
  Def: The controlled move from the current state to the new operating state.
-
  Term: Runbook
  Def: The timed plan of cutover tasks, owners, dependencies and fallback actions.
-
  Term: Hypercare
  Def: The period of extra monitoring and support immediately after cutover.

title: Meeting before
Plan quality
text:
- What outcome does this activity support?
- Who owns it?
- When will it start and finish?
- What input or decision does it rely on?
- What output will it produce?
- What conditions prove it is complete?
- Who receives or accepts the output?
- What happens if it is late?

title: Playbook
text:
-
  Title: Before accepting the detailed plan
  Items:
    - Does each activity support a clear outcome?
    - Are owners, dates and dependencies agreed?
    - Are acceptance criteria clear?
    - Has resource capacity been tested?
    - Do workstream dates support programme milestones?
    - Are testing, readiness, cutover and handover activities included?
-
  Title: Before the weekly workstream meeting
  Items:
    - Is the detailed plan current?
    - Which dates or forecasts changed?
    - Are actions, risks, issues and dependencies up to date?
    - Which items are overdue or ageing?
    - What decisions are needed, from whom and by when?
    - Does the Workstream Lead agree the proposed status?
-
  Title: Before reporting progress
  Items:
    - Does status reflect forecast and evidence rather than activity?
    - Are completion claims supported by acceptance criteria?
    - Are cross-workstream dependencies visible?
    - Are recovery actions realistic and owned?
    - Are cost, resource or customer effects included?
    - Is the programme ask clear?
-
  Title: Before raising an issue or decision
  Items:
    - What happened or may happen?
    - Which outcome, control, cost or date is affected?
    - What evidence supports the view?
    - What options and recovery actions exist?
    - Who owns the decision?
    - What is the last useful decision date?

title: Playbook
text:
-
  Title: Before changing the plan
  Items:
    - Is this a factual update or a change to the approved baseline?
    - Has the accountable owner made the decision?
    - Have scope, cost, timing and dependency effects been assessed?
    - Is the decision recorded?
    - Have all affected plans and logs been updated?
    - Have affected owners been told?
-
  Title: Before readiness or cutover
  Items:
    - Are readiness conditions linked to evidence and approvals?
    - Are defects, workarounds and remaining risks visible?
    - Are runbook tasks, owners and dependencies current?
    - Have fallback actions and checkpoints been agreed?
    - Is the status consistent with the evidence?
    - Are open actions controlled through hypercare or normal teams?

title: Principles
text:
- Keep one controlled and current workstream plan.
- Report forecast and evidence, not activity alone.
- Make every owner, dependency and completion condition clear.
- Challenge weak information without taking the decision.
- Keep the Workstream Lead accountable for priorities and outcomes.
- Raise issues before recovery time disappears.
- Control changes before updating the baseline.
- Turn every decision into recorded action.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: A workstream priority must change, but scope and programme dates are unaffected. Who should make the priority decision?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: The Workstream Project Manager, because the change affects the detailed plan.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: The Workstream Lead, using the planning impact prepared by the Project Manager.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: The Central PMO, because it owns the integrated programme plan.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: The Workstream Executive, because every baseline movement needs executive approval.
  Answer: B
  Feedback: The Workstream Lead owns workstream priorities. The Project Manager shows the delivery effect and records the decision.
-
  Q: An owner reports an activity as complete, but required approval is missing. What should the plan show?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: Complete, with approval recorded as a separate follow-up action.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: Complete for production and incomplete for readiness.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Not complete against the agreed acceptance criteria, with the approval owner and forecast date shown.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: The percentage complete selected by the activity owner.
  Answer: C
  Feedback: Completion depends on the agreed conditions and evidence, not only on production activity.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: When should a dependency be raised to the Central PMO?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: When it affects or may affect another workstream or a programme milestone and cannot be resolved within the workstream.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: As soon as another workstream owns any input to the detailed plan.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Only after both Workstream Leads confirm that the programme date will move.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: When the supplying workstream misses the agreed delivery date.
  Answer: A
  Feedback: Raise the dependency while the programme can still coordinate recovery. Keep routine interfaces within the workstream route where they remain controlled.
-
  Q: The Workstream Lead expects an evidence gap to close before reporting. What is the Project Manager's role?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: Accept the Lead's judgement and keep the gap out of reporting unless the deadline is missed.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: Set the status independently using the agreed reporting definition.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: Show the evidence, forecast and decision point so the Workstream Lead can confirm an informed status.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: Ask the Central PMO to determine the workstream rating.
  Answer: C
  Feedback: The Project Manager provides a controlled, evidence-based view. The Workstream Lead remains accountable for the workstream status.

title: Questions
text:
-
  Q: A proposed requirement adds value but also adds cost and time. What should happen before it enters the plan?
  Options:
    -
      Key: A
      Text: The Workstream Lead should confirm that the value justifies the change.
    -
      Key: B
      Text: The Project Manager should add a provisional activity so the delivery effect remains visible.
    -
      Key: C
      Text: The team should complete enough design to replace the estimate with a fixed cost.
    -
      Key: D
      Text: The change should be assessed and approved through the agreed authority using its cost, timing and delivery effects.
  Answer: D
  Feedback: A useful requirement is not automatically approved. The Project Manager controls the assessment and record while the authorised owner decides.
