title: Governance roles
text:
-
  Id: executive-sponsor
  Title: Executive Sponsor (Accountable Exec, AE)
  Tier: Sponsorship
  One Liner: Provide overall strategic direction and drive decision making at the highest levels
  Responsibilities: Ultimately responsible for the strategic and commercial success of the transaction
  Mandate: Makes Absa-wide, transaction-level decisions which may materially impact the shape or success of the transaction
  Prerequisites:
    - Must be empowered to convene top decision makers at short notice
    - Must be empowered to make decisions which impact the strategic direction of the transaction as a whole

title: Governance roles
text:
-
  Id: transaction-director
  Title: Transaction Director (TD)
  Tier: Transaction leadership
  One Liner: Senior leader accountable for the successful execution of the transaction. Translates the strategic intent and contractual requirements into an executable programme, establishes the organisation and governance to deliver it, and drives towards successful Legal Day 1
  Responsibilities: Translating the deal into an executable transaction programme, mobilising the transaction, owning the integrated execution plan, and leading programme governance and decision-making
  Mandate: Makes transaction-level decisions which are vital for execution, assesses intra-transaction trade-offs, and provides execution-level strategic direction
  Prerequisites:
    - Must be empowered to make transaction-level decisions related to execution
    - Must own the budget, to ensure the programme is staffed correctly
    - Must own the maintenance of the business case, to ensure the programme is tracking effectively
    - Must be empowered to escalate to executives at short notice on urgent matters
  Boundaries:
    - Accountable but not responsible for driving execution (Prog. Manager)
    - Escalates to AE where decisions have a broader strategic impact
    - Functional decisions on execution-specifics (design decisions, etc.) are made by Workstream Execs

title: Governance roles
text:
-
  Id: programme-manager
  Title: Programme Manager / Director
  Tier: Delivery leadership
  One Liner: Drives the day-to-day management and control of the M&A programme. Acts as the central point of coordination across the transaction, ensuring that plans, dependencies, risks, decisions and readiness are managed consistently across the organisation.
  Responsibilities: Establishes and operates the programme management framework, owns and maintains the integrated programme plan, drives cross-workstream coordination and dependency management, runs governance, reporting and decision support, leads the PMO and maintain delivery discipline
  Mandate: Makes programme-management related decisions, regarding the governance and execution of the plan (e.g. governance cadence, reporting structures, etc)
  Prerequisites:
    - Must be empowered to define the programme structure and governance
    - Must be empowered to hold execution teams accountable, regardless of seniority
    - Must drive plan creation, to ensure plan tracking is achievable and realistic
    - Must be empowered to escalate to the Transaction Director at short notice on urgent matters
  Boundaries:
    - Responsible for driving execution, but not the execution itself
    - Escalates to TD where decisions have a broader programme impact

title: Governance roles
text:
-
  Id: pmo-support
  Title: PMO Support
  Tier: Delivery leadership
  One Liner: Provides the programme management coordination, administration and control required to support delivery of an M&A deal
  Responsibilities: Maintains programme plans and milestone tracking, coordinates workstream reporting, maintains RAID logs, coordinates governance and programme forums, supports dependency and cross-workstream coordination, maintains programme documentation and controls
  Mandate: Limited decision mandate, may make decisions on escalations if execution is lacking
  Prerequisites:
    - Must be empowered to build relationships with Workstream Leads and hold them accountable, regardless of seniority
  Boundaries:
    - Responsible for coordinating execution, but not the execution itself
    - Escalates to Programme Manager where decisions must be made

title: Governance roles
text:
-
  Id: workstream-exec
  Title: Workstream Exec
  Tier: Delivery
  One Liner: Owns the success of the workstream outcomes and is ultimately accountable for their execution
  Responsibilities: Unblock workstream execution by providing SME input and decision making, support WSL with escalations and senior-level coordination, assure workstream trade-offs and major prioritisation decisions
  Mandate: Makes workstream-level prioritisation and trade-off decisions, signs off on key design decisions and workstream execution plan
  Prerequisites:
    - Must be empowered to define the strategic direction of the workstream, aligned to deal objectives
  Boundaries:
    - Accountable for workstream execution, not responsible
    - Escalates to AE / TD where trade-off decisions are programme-wide

title: Governance roles
text:
-
  Id: workstream-lead
  Title: Workstream Lead (WSL)
  Tier: Delivery
  One Liner: Defines and manages the backlog of work within their workstream, ensuring alignment with deal objectives
  Responsibilities: Own workstream scope, detailed plan, outcomes and deliverables. Develop and maintain the detailed workstream plan, mobilise and coordinate functional resources and SMEs, manage workstream risks, issues, assumptions and dependencies
  Mandate: Can determine workstream-level requirements, and make prioritisation decisions which do not impact overall delivery scope
  Prerequisites:
    - Must be empowered to define the detailed activities which sit underneath high-level milestones
    - Must be able to define resource requirements, and prioritise resource capacity
  Boundaries:
    - Responsible for driving workstream execution, and some of the execution itself
    - Escalate to Workstream Exec where trade-off decisions must be made

title: Governance roles
text:
-
  Id: workstream-project-manager
  Title: Workstream Project Manager
  Tier: Delivery
  One Liner: Supports the Workstream Lead by providing project management discipline, including tracking progress, managing timelines, reporting risks and issues, and coordinating across teams
  Responsibilities: Act as facilitator between the Workstream Lead and technical or operational teams to ensure smooth execution, own the coordination of the L2 plan, own workstream-level governance activities, and preparing WSL to report into Central Hub
  Mandate: Minimal decision making mandate
  Prerequisites:
    - none
  Boundaries:
    - Responsible for coordinating workstream execution, and some of the execution itself
    - Escalates to Workstream Lead where any decisions must be made
-
  Id: workstream-team-member
  Title: Workstream Team Member
  Tier: Delivery
  One Liner: Completes execution tasks within a workstream, and flags RAID items for escalation
  Responsibilities: Leverage function-specific SME knowledge to execute an plan and milestones, input into requirements and planning, escalate into workstream governance where needed
  Mandate: Minimal decision making mandate
  Prerequisites:
    - none
  Boundaries:
    - Responsible for actual execution, not decision making

title: Resourcing
text:
Minimum:
  -
    Role: Executive sponsor

  -
    Role: Transaction director

  -

  -

  -

  -

text:
Dedicated:
  -
    Role: Programme director / manager
    Note: One deal at a time
  -
    Role: Cutover manager
    Note: One deal, from readiness through hypercare
  -
    Role: Core PMO
    Note: One deal while the deal is live
  -
    Role: Regional lead in an in-scope country
    Note: One deal during execution peak

title: Spokes
text:
-
  Id: change-management
  Name: Change Management
  Conditional: true
  Purpose: Land the change with colleagues and leaders on both sides of the deal.
  Milestones:
    -
      Name: Change impact baseline agreed
      Activities:
        - Map impacted populations by function and country
        - Assess change load against business-as-usual calendars
        - Agree leader roles and cascade approach
        - Define adoption measures and readiness criteria
        - Confirm union and works-council touchpoints where relevant
    -
      Name: Business ready to operate the new model
      Activities:
        - Deliver leader and colleague readiness sessions
        - Run role and process walkthroughs
        - Confirm day-one support and floorwalker cover
        - Capture readiness evidence for go/no-go
        - Track adoption through hypercare and close gaps
  Dependencies:
    - HR for people perimeter
    - Ops for process design
    - Comms for cascade timing
  Delay Impact:
    - Colleagues unprepared at cutover, driving avoidable operational incidents
    - Adoption slips and benefit realisation moves out
  Local Knowledge: Country labour culture, language needs and local leadership structures.
  External Support: Capacity for large multi-country cascades; occasional specialist advice.

title: Spokes
text:
-
  Id: comms
  Name: Communications / Marketing
  Purpose: Control internal and external messaging across the deal timeline.
  Milestones:
    -

title: Operations & Servicing
text:
Key Role: Owns the operational service model, process hand-offs and client-servicing readiness for the transferring or retained book
Responsibilities:
  - Map current and target client journeys, servicing processes, operational controls and exception paths.
  - Define LD1 operating arrangements, including interim manual workarounds, non-BAU controls and temporary service procedures
  - Coordinate with Product, Technology, Data Migration and KYC / AML to turn business requirements into operationally workable processes
  - Confirm front-line, back-office and country teams can service clients and manage exceptions from LD1.
  - Own operational readiness evidence, service-level assumptions and hypercare handover to BAU owners.
  - Support Client readiness with executing onboarding activities
Boundary Items:
  - Product owns proposition and product design decisions
  - Technology owns system delivery; Operations owns process use, controls and service procedures
  - Client readiness coordinates overall LD1 evidence and onboarding tracking; Operations owns execution of onboarding and outreach
Central Hub Relationship: Relationship with Central Hub: the SA Functional Spoke owns operations and servicing decisions and evidence while the Central Hub sets programme standards, coordinates dependencies and escalates transaction-wide issues.

title: Operations & Servicing
text:
Regional Relationship:
  - Regional Spokes should own local execution as a minimum, with ownership scaling based on maturity, including process walkthroughs, servicing readiness, exception handling, control evidence, LD1 support and local issue resolution where they have capacity and delegated authority.
  - Function Authority retains operational standards, non-BAU control expectations, group service model decisions, central challenge and execution ownership where regional maturity, capability or capacity is insufficient.
  - As regional maturity increases, local ownership should expand from process evidence into operational remediation, readiness sign-off, cutover execution and hypercare support, with Function Authority retaining standards, specialist challenge and reserved approvals.
External Dependencies: External or counterparty dependencies are managed through the Central Hub governance route where timing, data, approvals or joint readiness affect LD1.

  Name: Current-state inventory and fit-gap assessment completed (5 weeks)

    - Map client permissions, account and mandate requirements, process hand-offs, volumes, service levels and exception paths.

  Name: Target service model and operating procedures approved (6 weeks)
  Activities:
    - Define the LD1 client journey, front-to-back process, operating roles, hand-offs, service standards and control points.
    - Document procedures for onboarding, servicing, transaction processing, complaints, queries, reporting and operational exceptions.

  Name: Cutover, discrepancy and manual-workaround plans approved (4 weeks)
  Activities:
    - Define blackout periods, cut-off times, transaction handling, data freezes, work allocation and command-centre support.
    - Create controlled procedures for discrepancies, failed onboarding, unsettled items, suspense balances and unsupported system activity.
    - Approve temporary manual workarounds, compensating controls, volumes, owners, expiry dates and escalation thresholds.

  Activities:
    - Confirm client, account, channel, product-linking, data, record, staffing and support readiness before go / no-go.
    - Operate LD1 and hypercare support with clear triage, service reporting, issue ownership and client-impact escalation.
    - Transfer residual workarounds, defects, service risks and improvement actions to named BAU owners with closure dates.

title: Procurement
text: Key Role: Owns procurement execution, supplier continuity and third-party contracting readiness for transferred, retained, replaced or transitional services, with country teams owning local supplier nuance and local contract execution where required.

title: Procurement
text:
Responsibilities:
  - Build supplier, contract, spend, purchase order, renewal, obligation, criticality and dependency inventories for the in-scope perimeter.
  - Confirm which supplier contracts transfer, terminate, require replacement, need novation, rely on TSA arrangements or remain with Absa.
  - Apply SA procurement policy and third-party risk standards, with in-country procurement customising execution for local supplier nuance, regulation and contracting practice.
  - Coordinate supplier categorisation and decisioning with the programme team, including the split between global framework agreements, central sourcing and local vendor onboarding.
  - Assess outsourcing, resilience, concentration, data, cyber, financial-crime, cost and regulatory third-party risks.
  - Manage vendor onboarding, supplier engagement, contract replacement, vendor consolidation and supplier exit activity where required for LD1 or TSA exit.
  - Confirm purchase-to-pay, approval, payment, supplier-management and supplier-risk processes operate from LD1 and through TSA exit.
  - Maintain visibility of programme decisions that affect supplier timing, contract scope, regulatory approval, information sharing, resourcing or onboarding lead times.
  - Escalate late procurement involvement, short-notice deadlines, missing supplier information or underestimated resource requirements before they create LD1 risk.

title: Procurement
text:
Boundary Items:
  - Legal owns contract drafting, novation legal advice, formal consents and legal restrictions on sharing existing contract information.
  - Technology owns technical supplier requirements, systems access, cyber integration and technology-service acceptance.
  - Operations & Servicing owns operational supplier use, service acceptance and day-one continuity requirements.
  - Finance & Tax owns spend baselining, payment-route design, cost allocation, stranded-cost analysis, Group Interchange charging, recharges and buy-back mechanics.
  - The Central Hub owns integrated TSA tracking, decision visibility and dependency escalation; Procurement owns the supplier action plan and evidence.
Central Hub Relationship: Relationship with Central Hub: Procurement owns supplier and third-party readiness decisions and evidence while the Central Hub coordinates cross-workstream dependencies, tracks programme decisions, challenges late escalations and holds owners accountable.

title: Procurement
text:
Regional Relationship:
  - Regional Spokes should own local execution as a minimum, with ownership scaling based on maturity, including local supplier data, vendor onboarding, local contracting steps, supplier engagement and local regulatory or market nuance where they have capacity and delegated authority.
  - Function Authority retains procurement policy, sourcing standards, global framework or group supplier decisions, third-party risk standards and execution ownership where regional maturity, capability or capacity is insufficient or a central supplier relationship must be protected.
  - As regional maturity increases, local ownership should expand from supplier evidence and execution support into vendor onboarding, local contracting and supplier-management activity, with Function Authority retaining central standards, specialist challenge and reserved approvals.
External Dependencies: External or counterparty dependencies are managed through the Central Hub governance route where supplier data, regulatory approval timing, contract sharing restrictions, buyer readiness or TSA terms affect LD1.

title: Mandate Rows

-

  Area: Procurement scope and supplier perimeter

  Hub Role: Coordinates dependency mapping and tracks open supplier decisions in the integrated plan.

  Escalation: Business commits to supplier choices before Procurement is involved, or programme decisioning changes supplier timing.

title: Product (Business)
text:
Key Role: Owns product proposition decisions and functional requirements for the portfolio, business or retained customer base


Note: For more complex deals, each business area or product may have its own workstream (Markets, Payments, Cards, Wealth, etc.). The roles, responsibilities, capabilities, and broad activities herein still apply.
Responsibilities:
  - Analyse the transferring, retained or acquired product set, including terms, pricing, features, eligibility, mandates and controls
  - Define product build, adaptation, withdrawal, migration, servicing and client-treatment requirements
  - Own product functional requirements and front-office process design with Operations & Servicing and Technology.
  - Act as business SMEs to input into testing, client communications inputs and readiness evidence
  - Lead the business execution of cutover activities to enable client transaction on LD1
  - Decide product exceptions, remediation or exclusions within delegated authority and escalate product risk
  - Support Technology in turning product business requirements into actionable technology requirements which support delivery
Boundary Items:
  - Risk / Credit owns risk appetite and credit decisions.
  - Operations & Servicing owns operational procedures and servicing model
  - Technology owns system delivery based on business-approved requirements.

title: Product (Business)
text:
Central Hub Relationship: Relationship with Central Hub: the Functional Spoke owns product proposition and requirements decisions and evidence while the Central Hub sets programme standards, coordinates dependencies and escalates transaction-wide issues.
Regional Relationship:
  - Regional Spokes should own local execution as a minimum, with ownership scaling based on maturity, including product evidence, pricing and terms nuance, customer impact input, local remediation and proposition readiness where they have capacity and delegated authority.
  - Function Authority retains proposition design, product standards, central product decisions, requirements, exception management and execution ownership where regional maturity, capability or capacity is insufficient.
  - As regional maturity increases, local ownership should expand from evidence and market input into local product-readiness activity, exception remediation and customer-impact execution, with Function Authority retaining standards, specialist challenge and reserved approvals.

title: Centralisation principles
text:
Remain Central Intro: What should remain central regardless of country maturity:
Remain Central:
  - Group-wide transaction governance, methodology, programme standards, issue escalation and executive reporting.
  - Material risk acceptance, group policy interpretation, group technology architecture and enterprise-level regulatory decisions.
  - Cross-border dependencies, transaction-wide readiness, cutover command centre, independent assurance and lessons learned.
  - SPA execution implications, TSA governance, completion-critical dependencies and cross-workstream dependency management.
Delegated Locally Intro: What can increasingly be delegated locally as maturity increases:
Delegated Locally:
  - Local process design, local stakeholder engagement, country-specific regulatory inputs and local execution planning.
  - Local readiness evidence, local testing participation, client or employee engagement execution and country issue resolution.
  - Routine operational decisions within delegated authority and within group standards.

title: Cross cutting minimum
text:
- A named accountable executive and named lead for each activated workstream.
- Sufficient protected capacity, with BAU backfill where transaction activity is material.
- Basic project-management capability: planning, dependencies, status reporting, issue escalation and evidence management.
- Clear delegated authority and an understood escalation route to the central Function Authority.
- Local legal, regulatory, cultural and market knowledge.
- Documented decisions, handovers, readiness evidence and residual-risk ownership

title: Maturity dimensions
text:
-
  Dimension: Functional expertise
  Low: Limited transaction or specialist capability; local team relies on SA SMEs.
  Medium: Competent BAU specialists with targeted transaction support.
  High: Experienced functional leads able to lead local transaction delivery.
-
  Dimension: Previous M&A experience
  Low: Limited or no comparable execution experience.
  Medium: Some change or transaction experience.
  High: Repeated M&A, migration, integration or separation experience.
-
  Dimension: Local decision authority
  Low: Low delegated authority and frequent SA approval needs.
  Medium: Delegated authority for routine operational decisions.
  High: Authority for local functional decisions within group policy.
-
  Dimension: Capacity
  Low: Thin capacity with BAU constraints.
  Medium: Named leads with some ring-fenced capacity.
  High: Dedicated local leads and support capacity for transaction delivery.
-
  Dimension: Process and governance quality
  Low: Processes poorly documented or inconsistently evidenced.
  Medium: Processes documented with some evidence gaps.
  High: Stable controls, clear governance and transaction-ready evidence.
-
  Dimension: Regulatory capability
  Low: Limited local regulatory engagement capability.
  Medium: Understands local requirements and needs central support for complex positions.
  High: Can lead local regulatory inputs and defend local readiness evidence.

title: Maturity dimensions
text:
-
  Dimension: Data and MI quality
  Low: Data quality issues and manual MI.
  Medium: Usable MI with defined remediation needs.
  High: Reliable MI, clear ownership and strong reconciliation discipline.
-
  Dimension: Artefact production
  Low: Requires templates and hands-on drafting support.
  Medium: Can produce drafts for central challenge.
  High: Can independently produce local plans, evidence and decision papers.

title: Minimum capability intro
text: The following defines the minimum country capability required to support transaction delivery. The level of local ownership should increase with maturity, capability, capacity and delegated authority, while reserved matters remain with the relevant Function Authority or central governance.

title: Regional key activities
text:
-
  Activity Type: Transaction set-up
  Centrally Led: Archetype classification, programme standards, governance design and integrated plan baseline.
  Jointly Delivered: Workstream charters and readiness criteria.
  Locally Led: Local mobilisation, local stakeholder mapping and local plan detail.
-
  Activity Type: Functional design
  Centrally Led: Group policy, architecture, control standards and transaction-wide decisions.
  Jointly Delivered: Process, product, technology, data and control design where local variants matter.
  Locally Led: Local process details, local customer journeys and country-specific execution methods.
-
  Activity Type: Execution
  Centrally Led: Critical-path coordination, cross-workstream dependencies and executive escalation.
  Jointly Delivered: Support provided by central teams where in-country do not have the maturity to deliver
  Locally Led: As much execution as is feasible for the in-country teams
-
  Activity Type: Readiness and cutover
  Centrally Led: Go/no-go pack, cutover command centre and transaction-level readiness decision.
  Jointly Delivered: Support provided by central teams where in-country do not have the maturity to deliver
  Locally Led: As much execution as is feasible for the in-country teams
-
  Activity Type: Hypercare
  Centrally Led: Transaction-wide stability dashboard and BAU handover governance.
  Jointly Delivered: Support provided by central teams where in-country do not have the maturity to deliver
  Locally Led: As much execution as is feasible for the in-country teams

title: Regional mandate

title: Regional responsibilities
text:
-
  Maturity: Country baseline
  Central Hub: Leads programme control, dependency management and local escalation. Provides more hands-on coordination.
  Functional Spoke: Leads functional design, planning, evidence standards and key execution tasks.
  Regional Spoke: Provides local data, stakeholder access, market insight and execution support.
-
  Maturity: More mature
  Central Hub: Maintains central governance, plan control, readiness integration and escalation.
  Functional Spoke: Sets standards, reviews local outputs and co-delivers complex tasks.
  Regional Spoke: Leads defined local activities and produces evidence for central review.
-
  Maturity: Most mature
  Central Hub: Maintains transaction-wide control, reserved authority and executive reporting.
  Functional Spoke: Provides standards, challenge, specialist input and escalation support.
  Regional Spoke: Leads local execution, local decision papers and readiness evidence within delegated authority.

title: Regional role profiles
text:
-
  Maturity: Country baseline
  Profile: Local coordinator, local SME and business contact who can provide facts, access and local logistics.
  Support Model: Central Centre of Excellence provides hands-on leadership, templates, drafting support and detailed review.
-
  Maturity: More mature
  Profile: Local workstream lead with BAU functional expertise and enough authority to coordinate local delivery.
  Support Model: Joint execution. Central Centre of Excellence provides standards, specialist challenge and review of key outputs.
-
  Maturity: Most mature
  Profile: Experienced local functional lead able to own local plans, evidence, decisions and stakeholder engagement.
  Support Model: Local lead executes within delegated authority. Central Centre of Excellence provides challenge, specialist escalation and group alignment.

title: Risk
text:
Key Role: Owns independent 2LOD risk oversight, risk appetite challenge and programme risk assurance, while business and functional owners remain accountable for 1LOD execution and control operation.
Responsibilities:
  - Confirm the 1LOD / 2LOD accountability model at mobilisation: business owns execution and controls; Risk owns independent oversight, challenge and escalation.
  - Define the role of in-country risk for country-based activity, including 2LOD oversight, local evidence, local governance input and support to central Risk.
  - Assess risk appetite for the deal, portfolio, product, client, country, sector and transaction route, and present material risk appetite items to board or exco where required.
  - Establish risk governance, principal risk type coverage, committee routes, evidence standards, risk acceptance process and escalation thresholds.
  - Challenge due diligence, control mapping, credit exposure analysis, data completeness, data accuracy, remediation actions and readiness evidence from 1LOD teams.
  - Coordinate risk input to assurance planning, including early scoping of Internal Audit, PwC, Deloitte, KPMG or other external assurers
  - Maintain independent risk views for signing, CP fulfilment, regulatory submissions, completion, LD1 go/no-go, hypercare and BAU transition.

title: Risk
text:
Boundary Items:
  - 1LOD business, functional and in-country owners own control design, remediation and local execution; Risk reviews, challenges, approves or escalates the residual risk position.
  - Compliance owns compliance interpretation and regulatory-condition tracking; Legal & CorpDev owns legal drafting and CP tracking; Risk owns the independent risk judgement and risk appetite route.
  - Independent Assurance and 3LOD Internal Audit provide assurance opinions; Risk should coordinate the overall assurance plan
  - Data Migration owns migration execution and reconciliation; Risk challenges whether the programme can evidence data completeness, accuracy and control operation.
  - E2E Testing and Client readiness own test execution and go-live orchestration; Risk challenges success criteria, evidence sufficiency and residual risk acceptability.
Central Hub Relationship: Relationship with Central Hub: Risk owns independent risk decisions, risk acceptances, appetite positions and readiness evidence while the Central Hub coordinates governance, issue tracking, integrated reporting and counterparty PMO escalation.

title: Risk
text:
Regional Relationship:
  - Regional Spokes should own local execution as a minimum, with ownership scaling based on maturity, including local 2LOD evidence, local governance input, control-owner challenge, MI and risk issue escalation where they have capacity and delegated authority.
  - Function Authority retains risk appetite, group risk standards, material risk acceptances, independent challenge, assurance coordination and execution ownership where regional maturity, capability or capacity is insufficient.
  - As regional maturity increases, local ownership should expand from evidence provision into local oversight, local committee input, readiness challenge and remediation tracking, with Function Authority retaining group standards, specialist challenge and reserved approvals.
External Dependencies: External or counterparty dependencies are managed through the Central Hub governance route where data, buyer readiness, regulator communication, external assurance, audit timing or risk evidence affects signing, completion or LD1.

title: Mandate Rows
text:
-
  Id: 1lod-2lod-accountability-and-risk-governance
  Area: 1LOD / 2LOD accountability and risk governance
  Spoke Authority:
    - Defines risk governance, risk acceptance route, principal risk type coverage and the 2LOD challenge model.
  Hub Role: Embeds risk cadence into programme governance and tracks actions to closure.
  Governance: Risk governance, accountable executive, programme SteerCo, board or exco where appetite requires.
  Escalation: Ownership between business, country Risk and central Risk is unclear or risk items are bypassing governance.
-
  Id: risk-appetite
  Area: Risk appetite
  Spoke Authority:
    - Approves or escalates risk appetite, policy exceptions, waivers and residual risk positions.
  Hub Role: Maintains plan visibility and tests timing against signing, CP and LD1 milestones.
  Governance: Enterprise Risk, principal risk type owners, board or exco where required.
  Escalation: Risk appetite is outside tolerance, data is incomplete, board/exco evidence is not ready or business case risk changes.

title: Mandate Rows
text:
-
  Id: external-assurance-scope-and-sequencing
  Area: External assurance scope and sequencing
  Spoke Authority:
    - Owns the risk view of assurance requirements and coordinates the appointment and sequencing conversation with IA, Compliance and external assurers.
  Hub Role: Maintains the integrated assurance calendar, evidence dependencies and escalation route. Inputs into assurance requirements based on SME knowledge
  Governance: Risk, Independent Assurance, Internal Audit, Compliance, Legal, Procurement where third-party assurance is relevant.
  Escalation: regulator-appointed assurance scope overlaps, arrives late
-
  Id: readiness-evidence-and-go-no-go-view
  Area: Readiness evidence and go/no-go view
  Spoke Authority:
    - Provides the independent risk opinion on mock runs, dress rehearsals, data completeness, digital readiness, cards readiness, controls and residual risk.
  Hub Role: Coordinates readiness pack, decision forum and open issue escalation.
  Governance: Client Readiness, E2E Testing, Data Migration, Operations, Technology, Compliance and programme SteerCo.
  Escalation: Success criteria are undefined, data comfort is not evidenced, or digital/cards readiness creates unmanaged LD1 risk.

title: Mandate Rows
text:
-
  Id: risk-issue-escalation-and-post-ld1-monitoring
  Area: Risk issue escalation and post-LD1 monitoring
  Spoke Authority:
    - Escalates material risks, monitors accepted risks and validates closure through cutover, hypercare and BAU transition.
  Hub Role: Tracks action owners, reporting cadence and accountable executive intervention.
  Governance: Risk committees, accountable executive, programme SteerCo, board/exco as needed.
  Escalation: SteerCos are cancelled, PMO issues are not front-run, residual risk rises, or risk acceptance pressure increases without evidence.

title: Risk

Capability Rows:

    Category: Specific Project Manager required?
    Content: Unlikely - simple balance sheet transactions can be coordinated through the Risk lead, and 2LOD risk oversight does not require significant technical coordination. Dedicated programme Risk coordinator or PM could be added as deal complexity increases, governance timelines tighten
  -
    Category: Baseline capabilities
    Content: 2LOD independent challenge; enterprise risk governance; risk appetite assessment; credit risk assessment; risk acceptance drafting; controls mapping; policy and process gap analysis; data-control review; readiness and go/no-go assurance.
  -

    Content: Principal risk type triage; acquired or sold policy mapping; local 1LOD execution assurance; integration, separation and standalone risk assessment; culture and maturity review; key-person dependency challenge; TSA and retained-service risk assessment.
  -
    Category: Specialist capabilities triggered by deal characteristics
    Content: Banking credit risk, insurance risk, operational resilience, conduct risk, regulatory risk, financial crime risk, cyber and technology risk, model risk, market and liquidity risk, reputational risk and country risk input where relevant.

title: Risk
text:

title: Milestones
text:
-
  Name: Risk appetite and due diligence assessment completed (4 weeks)
  Activities:
    - Confirm initial risk appetite fit for the portfolio, product, client, country, sector and transaction structure
    - Request due diligence inputs covering risk policies, control issues and incidents
    - Assess integration risk into the Absa environment, including risk policies, credit standards, data controls, processes, delegations and required waivers.
-
  Name: Risk governance and rules of engagement established (3 weeks)
  Activities:
    - Mobilise the Risk workstream with a named 2LOD lead, Enterprise Risk contact and principal risk type specialists as required
    - Define the risk accountability map, governance cadence, committee route and rules of engagement based on counterparty size, deal complexity and transaction perimeter.
    - Set evidence standards, committee lead times and escalation thresholds early so governance timelines are not underestimated

title: Milestones
text:
-
  Name: Principal risk type and control assessment completed (5 weeks)
  Activities:
    - Identify the principal risk types triggered by the transaction and engage relevant specialists early enough for formal review
    - Assess operational resilience, conduct, regulatory, financial crime, cyber, model, reputation, market and liquidity risks where the perimeter or product set requires it
    - Complete a culture and maturity risk assessment, including key-person dependency and operational capability risks that could affect readiness
    - Challenge business 1LOD workstream plans for governance requirements, data controls, control evidence, remediation actions and policy or process exceptions
-
  Name: Risk approvals and programme assurance kicked off (3 weeks)
  Activities:
    - Draft risk acceptances and waivers with clear owners, mitigations, expiry dates, monitoring requirements and escalation thresholds
    - Secure delegated Enterprise Risk approvals in time for signing, completion and LD1
    - Validate Central Hub SteerCo risk reporting and challenge understated severity, governance timing or readiness implications
    - Provide the Risk readiness view for testing exit, completion, LD1 go/no-go and BAU transition evidence packs.
    - Monitor residual risk through cutover and hypercare, with explicit control over late-stage pressure to accept risk without evidence

  - High-value or high-visibility deal which must be managed carefully
  - Deal scope impacts Absa’s fundamental regulatory processes (e.g., funding, capital adequacy, sanctions, AML reporting, etc.)
  - Multiple regulators involved with significant levels of scrutiny

title: Executive Sponsor (Accountable Executive, AE)
text:
Id: executive-sponsor
Heading: Executive Sponsor (Accountable Executive, AE)
Purpose: The Executive Sponsor is the senior executive accountable for the overall strategic, commercial and organisational success of the transaction. The role provides executive sponsorship, strategic direction and decision-making authority across the integration, separation or transition programme, ensuring that execution remains aligned to the deal rationale, business case and intended end-state. The Executive Sponsor acts as the ultimate internal escalation point for material transaction matters and ensures that the Transaction Director and programme team have the organisational authority, resources and executive support required to deliver the transaction successfully.
Reports To: Group / Business Executive Committee, CEO or relevant Board-level governance, depending on the transaction.
Direct Reports: Transaction Director and senior Executives responsible for major functional or business workstreams.

title: Executive Sponsor (Accountable Executive, AE)
text:
Core Responsibilities:
  - Set the strategic direction and success criteria for the transaction
  - Own executive accountability for the transaction outcome
  - Sponsor and empower the Transaction Director and programme leadership
  - Make or sponsor material transaction-level decisions
  - Resolve enterprise-level conflicts, blockers and resource constraints
  - Maintain alignment between execution, the business case and strategic intent
  - Chair or provide executive leadership into key transaction governance forums
  - Oversee material transaction risks, readiness and Go / No-Go decisions
  - Maintain executive and Board-level stakeholder alignment and sponsorship
  - Ensure the organisation remains committed to transaction priorities through execution

title: Executive Sponsor (Accountable Executive, AE)
text:
Success Measures:
  - Strategic alignment: The integration, separation or transition remains aligned to the transaction rationale, business case and intended operating model.
  - Executive decision effectiveness: Material decisions are made quickly, at the appropriate level, without unnecessary delay to the programme.
  - Organisational commitment: Business and functional leaders consistently prioritise transaction requirements and provide the resources needed to deliver.
  - Transaction outcome: The transaction achieves its intended strategic, commercial and operational objectives.
  - Risk oversight: Material risks are understood, appropriately mitigated or formally accepted by the relevant executive authority before key transaction milestones.
  - Governance effectiveness: The Transaction Director and programme team have clear sponsorship, decision rights and escalation routes throughout execution.
  - Readiness: Legal Day 1, Business Day 1 and other major transaction tollgates are supported by an evidence-based view of organisational readiness.
  - Value protection: Material threats to the business case, customer outcomes, synergies, stranded costs or other transaction economics are identified and addressed at executive level.
  - Stakeholder alignment: Executive Committee, Board and other senior stakeholders remain appropriately informed, aligned and supportive of the transaction.
  - Delivery sponsorship: Cross-functional conflicts, organisational barriers and resource constraints are resolved quickly enough to protect critical transaction milestones.

title: Executive Sponsor (Accountable Executive, AE)
text:
Experience Profile:
  - Senior executive leadership experience with sufficient organisational authority to make or sponsor enterprise-level decisions
  - Strong understanding of the organisation’s strategy, operating model and commercial priorities
  - Experience sponsoring complex, cross-functional transformation, M&A or other enterprise-critical programmes
  - Strong commercial judgement and ability to assess decisions in the context of the transaction business case and strategic rationale
  - Ability to operate effectively with incomplete information and make timely decisions under transaction deadlines
  - Strong understanding of executive governance, risk ownership and organisational accountability
  - Ability to challenge functional leaders and resolve competing business priorities
  - Confidence engaging with Board, Executive Committee, regulators and other senior stakeholders where required
  - Ability to sponsor difficult trade-offs across scope, timing, cost, risk and customer or employee outcomes
  - Strong judgement regarding which matters should remain delegated to the Transaction Director and which require executive intervention
  - Ability to secure organisational commitment, resource and funding for the transaction
  - Sufficient capacity and engagement to remain actively involved through major programme decisions, readiness tollgates, cutover and stabilisation

title: Transaction Director
text:
Id: transaction-director
Heading: Transaction Director
Purpose: The Transaction Director is the senior business-side leader accountable for the successful execution of the integration, separation or transition arising from an M&A transaction. The role translates the strategic intent and contractual requirements of the transaction into an executable programme, establishes the organisation and governance required to deliver it, and drives the business towards successful Legal Day 1, Business Day 1 and post-close stabilisation.
Reports To: Exec Sponsor
Direct Reports: Central PMO Office
Core Responsibilities:
  - Translate the deal into an executable transaction programme
  - Mobilise the transaction organisation
  - Own the integrated execution plan
  - Drive cross-functional execution and resolve barriers
  - Lead programme governance and decision-making
  - Manage the buyer/seller execution relationship
  - Own programme-level risk and readiness
  - Drive cutover, Day 1 and stabilisation

title: Transaction Director
text:
Success Measures:
  - Execution: Critical milestones achieved; dependencies actively managed; timely resolution of programme-level issues.
  - Readiness: Evidence-based Legal Day 1 and Business Day 1 readiness; critical testing completed; material residual risks understood and accepted.
  - Business continuity: Minimal disruption to customers, employees, suppliers and critical operations.
  - Transaction outcomes: Integration / separation decisions remain aligned to the strategic rationale and Target Operating Model.
  - Value protection: Synergies, stranded costs, TSA exits and other transaction economics remain visible and appropriately owned.
  - Governance: Decisions are made rapidly at the appropriate level with clear accountability and escalation.
  - Transition: Programme moves through cutover, stabilisation and handover without material uncontrolled residual risk.

title: Transaction Director
Programme Manager
text:
Id: programme-manager
Heading: Programme Manager
Purpose: The Programme Manager is responsible for the day-to-day management and control of the integration, separation or transition programme arising from an M&A transaction. The Programme Manager acts as the central point of coordination across the transaction, ensuring that plans, dependencies, risks, decisions and readiness are managed consistently across the organisation.
Reports To: Transaction Director
Direct Reports: PMO Support
Core Responsibilities:
  - Establish and operate the programme management framework
  - Own and maintain the integrated programme plan
  - Drive cross-workstream coordination and dependency management
  - Run governance, reporting and decision support
  - Own programme-level RAID, actions and change control
  - Coordinate buyer/seller programme execution
  - Coordinate readiness, testing and cutover management
  - Lead the PMO and maintain delivery discipline

title: Programme Manager
text:
Success Measures:
  - Plan quality: A credible and fully integrated programme plan exists, with clear owners, dependencies and critical-path milestones.
  - Delivery predictability: Slippage is identified early, recovery actions are established quickly and material surprises are minimised.
  - Cross-functional coordination: Dependencies and issues are resolved across organisational boundaries rather than remaining within individual workstreams.
  - Governance effectiveness: Executives receive concise, accurate information and decisions are made at the appropriate level and cadence.
  - Risk control: Material risks and issues have clear ownership, mitigation and escalation.
  - Readiness: Programme-level readiness assessments are evidence-based and inconsistencies between workstreams are surfaced before major tollgates.
  - Cutover preparedness: Cutover activities, dependencies, owners and escalation routes are understood and rehearsed.
  - Programme discipline: Workstreams consistently follow agreed planning, reporting and escalation processes.

title: Programme Manager
Central PMO Support
text:
Id: pmo-support
Heading: Central PMO Support
Purpose: Central PMO Support provides the programme management coordination, administration and control required to support delivery of an M&A integration, separation or transition programme.The role works under the direction of the Programme Manager to maintain the programme plan, governance, reporting, RAID management, actions, decisions and programme documentation.
Reports To: Programme Manager
Direct Reports: NA
Core Responsibilities:
  - Maintain programme plans and milestone tracking
  - Coordinate workstream reporting
  - Maintain RAID, actions and decision logs
  - Coordinate governance and programme forums
  - Support dependency and cross-workstream coordination
  - Support joint buyer/seller programme management
  - Support readiness, testing and cutover control
  - Maintain programme documentation and controls

title: Central PMO Support
text:
Success Measures:
  - Accuracy: Programme information is reliable, current and consistent across reporting artefacts.
  - Timeliness: Workstream reporting, governance materials and programme updates are produced to agreed deadlines.
  - Control: Risks, issues, actions, decisions and dependencies are visible and actively tracked.
  - Governance discipline: Forums receive the correct information and actions are followed through between meetings.
  - Plan integrity: Milestone and programme trackers reflect the latest agreed position.
  - Transparency: The Programme Manager and Transaction Director have a clear view of delivery status and emerging problems.
  - Documentation: Programme records are organised, accessible and provide an appropriate audit trail.
  - Delivery support: Workstream Leads spend less time on programme administration and more time resolving substantive delivery issues.

title: Central PMO Support
Workstream Lead
text:
Id: workstream-lead
Heading: Workstream Lead
Purpose: The Workstream Lead is accountable for the successful delivery of a defined functional or business workstream within an integration or separation programme. The Workstream Lead acts as the primary interface between their function, the central programme team and the equivalent workstream within the buyer or seller organisation.
Reports To: Programme Manager for delivery, with functional accountability to the Accountable Executive
Direct Reports: Functional SMEs, project managers and delivery resources assigned to the workstream
Core Responsibilities:
  - Own workstream scope, outcomes and deliverables
  - Develop and maintain the detailed workstream plan
  - Mobilise and coordinate functional resources and SMEs
  - Manage workstream risks, issues, assumptions and dependencies
  - Coordinate cross-workstream and buyer/seller dependencies
  - Drive functional decisions and escalate blockers promptly
  - Report workstream progress, readiness and exceptions to the central PMO
  - Own workstream readiness, testing and cutover activities

title: Workstream Lead
text:
Success Measures:
  - Delivery against plan: Workstream milestones and deliverables are completed to agreed scope, quality and timing.
  - Plan quality: A credible and sufficiently detailed workstream plan is maintained, with clear owners, dependencies and completion criteria.
  - Functional readiness: The workstream can evidence that people, processes, technology, data and controls within its scope are ready for the relevant transaction milestone.
  - Risk control: Material risks and issues are identified early, have clear mitigation plans and are escalated before they threaten programme outcomes.
  - Dependency management: Inputs required from other workstreams or the counterparty are identified early, actively managed and resolved to the required timeline.
  - Decision effectiveness: Functional decisions are taken quickly at the appropriate level, with unresolved matters escalated promptly.
  - Reporting discipline: Status, milestones, risks and dependencies are reported accurately and consistently to the central programme team.
  - Cutover preparedness: Workstream cutover activities, owners, sequencing, controls and contingency arrangements are understood, tested and ready for execution.

title: Workstream Lead
text:
Experience Profile:
  - Strong functional or business expertise within the relevant workstream area
  - Experience delivering complex change within the function, ideally in an M&A integration or separation environment
  - Ability to translate transaction requirements into detailed functional activities and deliverables
  - Strong planning, milestone and dependency management capability
  - Ability to identify and manage functional risks and issues proactively
  - Confidence coordinating senior SMEs and securing delivery from resources who may also have BAU responsibilities
  - Ability to work effectively across organisational and functional boundaries
  - Strong stakeholder management and communication capability
  - Ability to challenge assumptions and identify gaps in functional readiness
  - Experience working with technology, data, process and people dependencies relevant to the function
  - Ability to work constructively with the equivalent workstream within a buyer or seller counterparty while respecting pre-close information-sharing requirements
  - Strong judgement regarding when issues can be resolved within the workstream and when escalation to the Programme Manager, Transaction Director or Accountable Executive is required.

title: Success factors
text:
-
  Id: budget-ownership
  Number: 1
  Title: Clear financial / budget ownership
  Summary: The Transaction Director can spend the approved budget without line-item approvals.
  Decision Maker: Transaction Director
  Description:
    - The Transaction Director should be empowered to spend the approved budget as they see fit to drive transaction success.
    - Initial budget approval should be sought alongside CorpDev and the Accountable Executive, but once secured, approvals for individual line items should not be required.
  Impact:
    - Federated or unclear financial decision-making powers mean the transaction does not have the capacity and skills required to drive execution.
    - Heavy approval burdens slow decision-making and onboarding, placing the transaction at risk.

title: Success factors
text:
-
  Id: executive-buy-in
  Number: 2
  Title: Top-Down Executive buy-in
  Summary: Executives own outcomes in their areas and stay close enough to decide at short notice.
  Decision Maker: Accountable Executive
  Description:
    - Executives, including the Accountable Executive and Workstream Executives, must have direct ownership of outcomes within their areas.
    - They should be sufficiently close to execution to make decisions at short notice where required.
    - They should ultimately be held accountable for transaction outcomes within their area.
  Impact:
    - Workstreams lack sufficient strategic direction.
    - Delivery teams may become confused by multiple or competing priorities.
    - Executives may not be sufficiently involved to make key decisions quickly, increasing delivery timelines and execution risk.

title: Success factors
text:
-
  Id: capability-decision-making
  Number: 3
  Title: Capability decision making
  Summary: Workstream Leads can flag and close capability gaps early, with dedicated capacity where needed.
  Decision Maker: Workstream Leads
  Description:
    - Workstream Leads should be empowered to identify, flag and remediate capability or skills gaps as early as possible.
    - Workstream teams should have the capabilities required to execute successfully.
    - Dedicated capacity should be provided where required rather than simply repositioning internal roles; external specialists should be engaged where necessary.
  Impact:
    - Non-specialists may attempt specialist execution, increasing the likelihood that key issues are missed or identified late.
    - Workstream Leads may be unable to access the specialist support required to close capability gaps, increasing execution risk.

title: Success factors
text:
-
  Id: high-standards
  Number: 4
  Title: High standards, robustly maintained
  Summary: The Central Hub can challenge and reject sub-standard inputs, continuously and regardless of seniority.
  Decision Maker: Programme Manager
  Description:
    - The Central Hub must be able to hold the broader programme team to best-in-class execution, governance and reporting standards regardless of seniority.
    - The Programme Manager and PMO should be empowered to challenge and reject inputs that are not up to standard.
    - Challenge should happen continuously and should not wait for SteerCo meetings.
  Impact:
    - If the Central Hub cannot challenge directly, sub-standard reporting and execution may reach SteerCo and hamper effective decision-making.
    - Workstream Executives may spend unnecessary time resolving execution issues rather than focusing on strategic decisions.

title: Success factors
text:
-
  Id: business-leads-execution
  Number: 5
  Title: Business must lead execution, supported by the Central Hub
  Summary: Execution ownership sits in the Business Unit; the Hub coordinates, supports and challenges.
  Decision Maker: Workstream Executives
  Description:
    - Responsibility for execution must sit within the relevant Business Unit, even where a Workstream Lead is supported by a Programme Manager.
    - Workstream Leads should be business stakeholders rather than project managers and should understand the relevant SME knowledge and Business Unit ownership.
    - Workstream Executives should appoint appropriate senior business stakeholders as Workstream Leads to create ownership and buy-in.
    - The Central Hub / Programme Management team should provide coordination, support, check and challenge rather than taking ownership away from the business.
  Impact:
    - Business Units may not feel accountable for deal outcomes, reducing long-term ownership once the transaction moves into BAU.
    - Programme Managers may lack the detailed understanding of business processes required to properly plan and prioritise execution, increasing delivery risk.

title: Success factors
text:
-
  Id: direct-interface
  Number: 6
  Title: Direct interface into decision makers
  Summary: The Transaction Director can escalate straight to executives at short notice.
  Decision Maker: Transaction Director
  Description:
    - The Transaction Director must be empowered to escalate directly to the Accountable Executive and Workstream Executives at short notice when required.
    - Executives must prioritise transaction-related escalations and convene relevant decision makers.
    - Decisions should not be unnecessarily held until formal governance forums where they can be resolved earlier.
  Impact:
    - Slow and non-prioritised decision-making leaves issues unresolved and reduces the time available for remediation.
    - Lack of a clear, shared understanding of transaction importance and prioritisation can prevent the programme receiving sufficient executive attention.

title: Success factors
text:
-
  Id: bau-processes
  Number: 7
  Title: BAU processes should take on approved changes, in support of the deal
  Summary: BAU processes can be challenged and adapted for the transaction, with risks managed and changes signed off.
  Decision Maker: Accountable Executive
  Description:
    - Teams across the programme should be empowered to challenge BAU processes where those processes do not suit the transaction and are slowing execution.
    - The default position should be that processes can be adapted where appropriate, provided material risks are understood and managed.
    - Changes to BAU processes should be formally signed off by the appropriate Workstream / business ownership.
  Impact:
    - Teams may default to “the way things have always been done”, constraining the programme unnecessarily.
    - Existing processes may dictate the transaction approach rather than being challenged to achieve better outcomes.
    - This can result in slower execution, greater complexity and poorer outcomes.

title: Technology
text:
Key Role: Owns technology delivery required to support the transaction perimeter and target operating model, including environment readiness, architecture, solution design, build, testing, contingency planning, war-room escalation and service transition. Technology also supports capability mapping during due diligence, while business and Product Owners should own the target capability decisions in the future state.
Responsibilities:
  - Map current and required capabilities across digital channels, branch channels, core systems, integration points and operational platforms.
  - Translate business, product, operational, data and control requirements into technology scope, architecture decisions and solution design.
  - Deliver environments, build, configuration, interfaces, access, non-functional testing, release management and deployment plans.
  - Coordinate with Data Migration on source and target systems, data feeds, ETL environment needs, extract routines and cutover technical runbooks.
  - Define technology contingency, fallback, resilience, cyber, access and war-room escalation requirements for testing, cutover and hypercare
  - Maintain central visibility of resourcing contracts and technology delivery assumptions, including country-owned contract items such as travel, local support and implementation dependencies
  - Own technology service transition assessment, remediation, post-LD1 stabilisation and handover into BAU technology operations.

title: Technology
text:
Boundary Items:
  - Business and Product Owners own business capability requirements, target capability decisions and acceptance criteria; Technology performs capability mapping and feasibility assessment where Product Owner capability is not yet mature.
  - Data Migration owns migration logic, data quality, reconciliation and data cutover; Technology owns platforms, environments, interfaces, access and technical cutover.
  - Procurement owns supplier sourcing and third-party contract actions; Technology owns technical vendor requirements and must input to resourcing, travel and implementation contract terms before commitments are made.
  - Regional technology teams execute local activity where agreed, but central Technology owns or approves decisions affecting SA-hosted core systems and central accountability.
  - E2E Testing owns integrated journey coverage and evidence; Technology owns technical testing, environments, defect remediation and release readiness.
Central Hub Relationship: Relationship with Central Hub: the SA Functional Spoke owns technology delivery decisions, technical readiness evidence and technology budget or resourcing assumptions where it is accountable, while the Central Hub coordinates dependencies, governance cadence, scope control and escalation.

title: Technology
text:
Regional Relationship:
  - Regional Spokes should own local execution as a minimum, with ownership scaling based on maturity, including local system and infrastructure evidence, access coordination, local suppliers, testing support, deployment prerequisites and country implementation activity where they have capacity and delegated authority.
  - Function Authority retains architecture, SA-hosted core systems, cyber and access standards, central platforms, budget or resourcing accountability, and execution ownership where regional maturity, capability or capacity is insufficient.
  - As regional maturity increases, local ownership should expand from evidence and support into local delivery, test execution and deployment activity, with Function Authority retaining standards, specialist challenge and reserved approvals.
External Dependencies: External or counterparty dependencies are managed through the Central Hub governance route where technology data, environments, supplier contracts, access, approvals, buyer readiness or joint testing affect LD1.

title: Mandate Rows
text:
-
  Id: capability-mapping-and-target-technology-scope
  Area: Capability mapping and target technology scope
  Spoke Authority:
    - Maps current and required channel, core-system and platform capabilities where business or Product Owners do not have requisite capabilities
  Hub Role: Ensures capability decisions are captured in scope, plan, budget and dependency governance.
  Governance: Business owner, Product Owners, Architecture, Technology, Operations and programme governance.
  Escalation: Business capability ownership is weak, Product Owner capacity is unclear, or technology scope is being inferred without evidence.
-
  Id: technology-solution-architecture-and-delivery-route
  Area: Technology solution architecture and delivery route
  Spoke Authority:
    - Owns solution design, architecture decisions, lift-and-shift versus build recommendation, environment approach and non-functional requirements.
  Hub Role: Challenges critical path, dependency impact, scope control and readiness evidence.
  Governance: Architecture, Cyber, Risk, Compliance, Technology governance and programme SteerCo.
  Escalation: Architecture exception, cyber risk, target-state conflict, environment gap or local maturity issue threatens delivery.

title: Mandate Rows
text:
-
  Id: resourcing-budget-and-contracting-assumptions
  Area: Resourcing, budget and contracting assumptions
  Spoke Authority:
    - Owns technology delivery resourcing assumptions and should control or approve the technology budget where held accountable for outcomes.
  Hub Role: Tracks budget, procurement and dependency impacts across the integrated plan.
  Governance: Technology leadership, Finance & Tax, Procurement, HR where people capacity is required, and programme governance.
  Escalation: Country-owned contracts omit delivery needs, central Technology is accountable without decision rights, or run-cost uplift is not funded.
-
  Id: build-test-and-release-readiness
  Area: Build, test and release readiness
  Spoke Authority:
    - Approves build scope, release sequencing, environment readiness, test support and defect remediation for technology deliverables.
  Hub Role: Coordinates cross-workstream readiness, E2E dependency and issue escalation.
  Governance: Technology governance, change advisory controls, E2E Testing, Data Migration and Risk.
  Escalation: Testing fails without agreed learning path, change freeze applies, capacity is short or release evidence is incomplete.

title: Mandate Rows
text:
-
  Id: cutover-contingency-and-war-room-escalation
  Area: Cutover, contingency and war-room escalation
  Spoke Authority:
    - Defines technical cutover, contingency, fallback, resilience, war-room entry criteria and issue escalation route.
  Hub Role: Integrates technology cutover into the LD1 command centre and programme go/no-go pack.
  Governance: Client Readiness, Risk, Cyber, Operations, Data Migration and programme governance.
  Escalation: Fallback is not viable, technology incident affects wider Absa operations, or local teams make decisions outside agreed mandate.
-
  Id: service-transition-and-post-ld1-readiness
  Area: Service transition and post-LD1 readiness
  Spoke Authority:
    - Recommends technology readiness status, accepted exceptions, residual risk and BAU service transition approach.
  Hub Role: Integrates readiness and exceptions into completion, LD1 and hypercare governance.
  Governance: Technology operations, service management, Cyber, Risk, accountable business owner and BAU control owners.
  Escalation: Critical readiness evidence, service support, licensing, support staffing or residual exception remains unresolved at go/no-go.

title: Technology
text:
Capability Rows:
  -
    Category: Specific Project Manager required?
    Content: Yes - build, release, environment, access, testing, cutover and service-transition activity require dedicated technology PM support, with clear ownership of technology budget and resourcing assumptions where Technology is accountable.
  -
    Category: Baseline capabilities
    Content: Solution architecture, capability mapping, application delivery, environment management, integration, access, release control, cyber, resilience, technical testing and service transition.
  -
    Category: Incremental capabilities by deal archetype / complexity
    Content: Lift-and-shift versus build assessment, channel enhancement, core-system integration, platform transfer, data-migration enablement, supplier take-on, licensing uplift, country execution oversight and TSA exit.
  -
    Category: Specialist capabilities triggered by deal characteristics
    Content: Digital channels, branch channels, core banking, cards, payments, identity, cloud, cyber, regulatory technology, legacy wind-down, local infrastructure, vendor transition and run-cost modelling.
Milestone Intro:
  - The key milestones below are organised as a baseline set, with additional milestones required for more complex deal archetypes split out below as required.
  - As deal archetypes scale from balance sheet to partial business to full business, each baseline activity should be assessed against the complexity factors laid out in the deal archetype documentation.

title: Technology
text:
Service Catalogue:
  - Environment readiness
  - Architecture decision making and solution design
  - Technology contingency planning
  - War room planning and escalation
  - Technology build based on business or migration requirements
  - Technology testing coordination and execution
  - Technology service transition assessment and remediation

title: Balance Sheet Acquisition - baseline activities
text:
Id: balance-sheet-acquisition
Heading: Balance Sheet Acquisition - baseline activities
Tab: Balance Sheet Acquisition

title: Milestones
text:
-
  Name: Product mapping and capability assessment (7 weeks)
  Activities:
    - Assess current and required capabilities across digital, branch, core-system and operational channels during due diligence.
    - Recommend lift-and-shift, build, enhance, procure or decommission options based on target operating model and delivery feasibility.
    - Confirm that business or Product Owners make capability decisions, with Technology documenting feasibility and implications.
-
  Name: Technology build based on business or migration requirements (8 weeks)
  Activities:
    - Deliver build, configuration, interfaces, access, reporting, infrastructure and integration changes needed for the deal perimeter, based on capability gaps identified
    - Coordinate build with Data Migration requirements, supplier inputs, security controls and business acceptance criteria
    - Track scope changes, budget impact, licensing uplift and support-staff implications from build decisions.
-
  Name: Environment set up & maintenance (7 weeks)
  Activities:
    - Confirm environments, access, connectivity, test data, release windows and non-production controls required for the transaction.
    - Identify environment gaps affecting Data Migration, E2E Testing, Operations, Risk, Compliance and Client Readiness
    - Evidence environment stability, access readiness and support ownership before formal testing starts

title: Milestones
text:
-
  Name: Contingency planning & failover readiness (4 weeks)
  Activities:
    - Define resilience, fallback, rollback, manual workaround and incident paths for technology failure scenarios
    - Align contingency plans with Data Migration, Operations, Risk, E2E Testing and Client Readiness.
    - Confirm contingency owners, decision points and evidence before dress rehearsals and go-live.
-
  Name: War room protocol definition and testing (6 weeks)
  Activities:
    - Define war-room entry criteria, issue severity, escalation route, decision authority and command-centre participation.
    - Confirm central and country technology contacts, supplier contacts and out-of-hours support arrangements.
    - Agree which issues enter the war room and which move into backlog or BAU remediation.
-
  Name: Technology testing coordination and execution (6 weeks)
  Activities:
    - Run technical testing, SIT support, non-functional testing, defect remediation and release readiness checks.
    - Support E2E Testing with environments, data feeds, technical defect resolution and evidence for go/no-go.
-
  Name: Technology service transition assessment and remediation (3 weeks)
  Activities:
    - Assess BAU support model, service desk, monitoring, access support, incident management, capacity and run-cost requirements.
    - Remediate service-transition gaps before LD1 or agree accepted exceptions with accountable owners.
    - Transfer open technology issues to hypercare or BAU technology operations with clear ownership.

title: Milestones
breadcrumb: Full Business Acquisition B (standalone) - new activity set
text:
-
  Name: Standalone technology operating model and architecture designed (6 weeks)
  Activities:
    - Define standalone systems, channels, infrastructure, integration, support model, security and governance required for the acquired business.
    - Assess whether to take over existing technology, procure new platforms, build Absa-hosted capability or run interim TSA-backed services.

-
  Name: Core systems, channels and environments stood up (8 weeks)

    - Build or procure core systems, digital channels, branch channels, access, identity, infrastructure and operational platforms, as required, or assess suitability of existing
    - Set up environments, monitoring, release processes, service management and cyber controls.

title: Milestones
breadcrumb: Full Business Acquisition B (standalone) - new activity set
text:
-
  Name: Standalone test, contingency and cutover rehearsed (6 weeks)
  Activities:

    - Confirm market-specific testing approach, defect response and readiness evidence.
    - Update cutover and fallback plans based on rehearsal findings.
-
  Name: Standalone service transition completed (3 weeks)
  Activities:
    - Stand up BAU technology operations, support staffing, incident management, monitoring and vendor support.
    - Confirm licensing, support cost and run-cost uplift are reflected in Finance and operating budgets.
    - Transfer open technology actions to hypercare or standalone BAU owners.

title: Balance Sheet Sale - baseline divestment activities
breadcrumb: Balance Sheet Sale - baseline divestment activities
text:
Milestones:
  -
    Name: Technology sale perimeter and exit requirements defined (4 weeks)
    Activities:
      - Identify systems, channels, access, interfaces, data feeds, infrastructure and services affected by sale
      - Confirm Absa retained systems, buyer hand-off and technology exit obligations
      - Assess whether buyer support requires lift-and-shift, extract-only support, TSA services or temporary access.
  -
    Name: Buyer-facing technology support and data enablement prepared (8 weeks)
    Activities:
      - Provide technical input needed for buyer source-to-target mapping, data extraction, access setup and interface understanding.
      - Confirm confidentiality, security and access controls for buyer-facing technology support.
  -
    Name: Absa technology controls and cutover route agreed (6 weeks)
    Activities:
      - Plan access removal, interface shutdown, retained service continuity, release windows and technical fallback.
      - Run technical testing and cutover rehearsal for seller-side technology steps.
      - Confirm readiness evidence for completion, LD1 and post-LD1 support.
  -
    Name: Service transition and residual support handed over (3 weeks)
    Activities:
      - Define post-LD1 support model, defect ownership, service levels and escalation route.
      - Transfer buyer, Absa BAU or TSA technology issues to the right owner.
      - Close Absa technology exit actions once retained controls and support obligations are stable.

title: Activity Sets
text:
-
  Id: partial-business-sale
  Heading: Partial Business Sale - additional divestment activities
  Tab: Partial Business Sale
  Lead: The above, with the addition of:
  Milestones:
    -
      Name: Shared technology and TSA dependencies mapped (4 weeks)
      Activities:
        - Separate technology services, systems, access, interfaces and support between buyer, retained Absa and TSA-backed activity.
        - Confirm local country systems, contracts and support dependencies needed for the carve-out.
        - Map technology dependencies to Procurement, Data Migration, Operations, Risk and Legal obligations.
    -
      Name: Partial separation build, test and access controls completed (8 weeks)
      Activities:
        - Deliver access changes, interface changes, retained-system controls and buyer hand-off technology changes.
        - Test shared-service and TSA-supported journeys with E2E Testing and Client Readiness.
        - Validate that retained Absa systems remain stable and secure after separation.
    -
      Name: TSA exit technology path launched (4 weeks)
      Activities:
        - Define technology actions needed to exit TSAs, remove shared access and close temporary support.
        - Track buyer readiness and Absa residual technology risks through governance.
        - Confirm BAU or buyer ownership for post-LD1 defects and residual support.

title: Activity Sets
text:
-

      Activities:

        - Escalate buyer technology readiness gaps through joint governance.
    -
      Name: Absa exit controls and retained service readiness completed (4 weeks)
      Activities:
        - Execute access removal, interface changes, monitoring updates, retained platform controls and service continuity checks.
        - Support buyer integration testing where Absa systems or data are in scope.
        - Confirm technology readiness evidence for TSA entry, TSA exit and Absa retained obligations.

title: Activity Sets
text:

        - Define the buyer standalone technology capabilities, systems, channels, support, access and data enablement Absa must support.
        - Agree evidence Absa requires before service exit or obligation closure.
        - Confirm local country, supplier, security and regulatory technology dependencies.
    -
      Name: Full Absa technology separation executed (8 weeks)
      Activities:

      Name: Technology TSA exit and obligation closure completed (4 weeks)

    Text: The archetype is the first level of order applied to potentially infinite deal variables - classifying what the deal is trying to achieve into broad buckets of work correlated with what needs to be done

    - Archetypes are the first degree of order applied to a disparate system: classifying deals by their intended outcomes and objectives
    - Each archetype fundamentally changes where execution must focus,  driven by the deal perimeter, with complexity factors such as jurisdiction, product set, maturity, and regulatory landscape layered on top
