Id: operating-model
Label: Operating Model
Question: How do we deliver on our goals?
Heading: Operating Model is where this comes together
Sub Heading:
  Title: What is the Operating Model for?
  Text: The Operating Model takes what needs to be done, and returns how these things should be done by setting out  standardised structures for executing deals
Points:
  - The structure must remain largely the same across archetypes, to drive consistency and repeatability
  - What changes is what the workstreams must be focused on, the scale of their teams, and the key capabilities required

title: Principle
breadcrumb: Operating Model is where this comes together
text:
Label: Core principles
Title: How the operating model is built

title: Points
breadcrumb: Operating Model is where this comes together
text:
- The Operating Model is based on Hub & Spoke structure - A Central Hub is supported by regional and functional spokes, with ownership over differing parts of the transaction
- The Hub is a Centre of Excellence - The Hub ensures consistency of delivery quality and expertise across multiple deals
- In-Country Accountable Executives are accountable for successful go-live - Country stakeholders must be ultimately accountable for successful execution of integration to drive ownership
- Spokes are where delivery happens - The Spokes drive execution of the delivery activities critical to making go-live happen
- Within the Spokes in-country teams are responsible for local execution at a minimum
As much execution as possible should happen in-country, with the minimum standard being execution of items requiring local nuance. Execution responsibility increases based on country maturity, determined by centre teams
- Central functional Spokes will support execution where needed - Where in-country teams do not have the requisite skills or capabilities to deliver, central functions will support
- Clear accountability must sit with the teams that own the outcome - In-country and central teams should have explicit ownership for the decisions and delivery activities they control, with shared accountability where delivery is dependent on both
- Decisions should have a bias for speed
Where BAU decision-making processes are not fit for purpose, an alternative may need to be found without weakening the control fabric of the organisation.

title: Points
breadcrumb: Operating Model is where this comes together
text:
- Experienced colleagues must support new transactions
Absa colleagues who have gained experience of M&A transactions via previous deals have an obligation to support new deals by acting as an Experienced Coach

title: These are the principles guiding all of the work
breadcrumb: These are the principles guiding all of the work
text:
Label: Overarching principles
Title: These are the principles guiding all of the work
Points:
  - Retain standard non-M&A, execution methodologies
Existing Absa methodologies with established governance, controls and SME-led execution, such as Due Diligence, legal drafting, technology delivery and other functional processes, are not challenged or reworked. Instead, they are integrated into the M&A lifecycle, with a focus on how each function contributes to successful transaction delivery.
  - Maintain consistency where viable
Wherever possible, the lifecycles should have consistent stages, purposes, and areas of focus, to enable a consistent and repeatable M&A capability within Absa
  - Ground in experience, not theory - Lifecycles are based on best practice, but also on first hand experience on real deals. They are grounded in lived experience, rather than being academically built from first principles
  - Use tooling to accelerate, not replace, human judgement
Frameworks, templates and knowledge should help teams make faster, better-informed decisions, while experienced judgement remains critical to applying them in the context of each deal.

title: The M&A Capability Hub provides a single source of practical guidance for M&A execution.
breadcrumb: The M&A Capability Hub provides a single source of practical guidance for M&A execution.
text:
Title: The M&A Capability Hub provides a single source of practical guidance for M&A execution.
Body: The Hub enables Absa teams to deliver transactions by bringing together execution best practice, proven frameworks and expertise knowledge. It translates this knowledge into practical guidance, templates and tools that teams can use throughout the transaction lifecycle.
Items:
  -
    Title: A repeatable execution model
    Body: Moves Absa from individual-led, experience-based delivery to an institutional capability that can run more concurrent and more complex transactions
  -
    Title: Earlier, faster mobilisation
    Body: Mobilisation is guided by the deal archetype, so internal teams, regional Spokes and partners stand up quickly instead of starting from a blank page
  -
    Title: Clear ownership and governance
    Body: Named owners for each functional area, with the decision rights, structure and practical guidance needed to execute rather than side-of-the-desk effort
  -
    Title: Scalable partner capacity
    Body: Pre-agreed engagement models per functional area that can be activated to add capacity and close capability gaps as deal volume and complexity rise
  -
    Title: Proactive readiness
    Body: Mechanisms, tools and lessons that make each transaction a stronger starting point for the next, rather than a reactive rebuild
  -
    Title: Better predictability and risk management
    Body: Brings these capabilities together to give Absa greater predictability and control over risk, particularly when managing multiple transactions alongside BAU priorities

title: Page copy — /deal-governance
text:
[Route]
What changes as part of Deal Governance? | Absa M&A Capability Hub
The BAU processes that change for a transaction, what changes and why it must change.
What changes as part of Deal Governance?
How BAU processes adapt for a transaction, and why they must change.
[GROUPS]
Money and people
Budget approval
Approve an initial transaction budget and contingency centrally. Delegate spend decisions within defined thresholds to the Accountable Executive or Transaction Director instead of returning to normal budgeting forums. Retain Finance reporting and retrospective governance.
Deals require rapid mobilisation before requirements and costs are fully known. Waiting for standard budget cycles can delay diligence, signing, regulatory commitments or LD1 readiness.
Resource prioritisation
Give the transaction authority to secure named functional resources and resolve conflicts with BAU priorities. Escalate unresolved constraints directly to accountable functional executives.
Workstreams need scarce SMEs at the same time. Normal resource allocation often optimises within functions rather than for the transaction's critical path.
Headcount approval
Establish expedited approval for temporary hires, secondments and fixed-term resources within the transaction budget.
Programme capacity must often be added faster than permanent workforce-planning cycles allow.
Employee onboarding
Introduce a priority onboarding route for programme employees and contractors, with parallel rather than sequential checks where permitted. Mandatory screening remains unchanged.

title: Page copy — /deal-governance
text:
[GROUPS]
Delays in onboarding directly reduce the time available for design, testing, migration and readiness.
Performance objectives
Reflect transaction responsibilities in individual objectives and give programme commitments explicit priority against BAU deliverables.
Resources will continue to prioritise BAU obligations unless transaction accountability is formally recognised.
Suppliers, access and data
Contractor and adviser mobilisation
Use pre-approved panels, standard transaction terms and accelerated statements of work. Allow mobilisation at risk only under explicitly approved, limited conditions.
Legal, tax, technology, separation and integration expertise is often needed immediately and for a finite period.
Supplier onboarding
Prioritise vendor due diligence, system registration, banking validation and purchase-order creation. Run checks concurrently where possible.
Even after selection, BAU supplier onboarding can prevent critical vendors from beginning work or being paid.
Access provisioning
Establish a priority route for systems, premises, data-room and collaboration-tool access. Bundle access requests by role and pre-approve standard profiles.
New teams cannot contribute effectively while waiting through normal individual access-request queues.
Data sharing
Introduce an expedited approval route for sharing data between seller, buyer, advisers and countries, using approved transfer mechanisms and minimum-necessary datasets.
Diligence, planning, testing and migration depend on information moving across organisational and jurisdictional boundaries.

title: Page copy — /deal-governance
text:
[GROUPS]
Decisions, risk and escalation
Policy exceptions
Create a single, controlled exception process with a named owner, risk assessment, compensating controls, approval level and expiry date.
Multiple BAU exception routes are too slow and can produce inconsistent decisions across workstreams.
Functional decisions
Delegate operational decisions to Regional Spokes where they have the maturity, capability and capacity. Central functions decide or support where those conditions are not met.
Decisions need to be made close to execution without allowing capability gaps to create uncontrolled risk or delay.
Risk acceptance
Establish transaction-specific risk thresholds and delegated acceptance levels. Escalate material residual risks directly through programme governance.
Some risks cannot be eliminated before LD1; they must be explicitly assessed, owned and accepted within the transaction timetable.
Legal escalation
Route material legal interpretations, contractual constraints and unresolved liabilities directly to the Legal and CorpDev authority and transaction governance.
Standard escalation chains can be too slow where a legal issue affects signing, completion, perimeter or execution strategy.
Issue and dependency escalation
Introduce shorter escalation thresholds based on impact to signing, completion, LD1, customers, regulation, cost or reputation.
An issue that would be tolerable in BAU can become material when only days remain before a contractual milestone.
Technology, testing and change
Technology architecture approval

title: Page copy — /deal-governance
text:
[GROUPS]
Introduce dedicated architecture forums with shortened turnaround times, predefined principles and authority to approve temporary transition states.
A transaction may require interim architecture, duplicated services or TSAs that would not be accepted as a normal long-term design.
Technology change and release
Reserve transaction release windows and create an expedited release path while retaining testing, rollback, segregation-of-duties and cyber controls.
BAU release calendars may not align with legally fixed completion, migration and LD1 dates.
Testing governance
Prioritise transaction environments and test data. Permit risk-based test scope only where explicitly approved, with defects and residual risk recorded.
Fixed deadlines compress test cycles, but reducing testing without formal risk decisions can undermine operational readiness.
Operational change approval
Establish a cross-functional transaction change authority that can approve coordinated process changes across products, operations, technology and controls.
BAU change forums tend to consider changes function by function, while transaction outcomes depend on end-to-end readiness.
Business continuity and incident response
Create transaction-specific playbooks, command structures and escalation contacts covering cutover, migration and early-life support.
BAU incident procedures may not address split accountability, TSAs, seller dependencies or newly transferred operations.
Communications, reporting and assurance
Customer and colleague communications

title: Page copy — /deal-governance
text:
[GROUPS]
Use accelerated drafting, approval and release processes with pre-agreed approvers, templates and regulatory review points.
Communications may be triggered by signing, regulatory approval, completion or leaks and may require immediate coordinated release.
Management reporting
Replace normal reporting cycles with a single programme cadence, standard status definitions, integrated milestones and exception-based reporting.
Weekly or monthly BAU reporting does not provide enough visibility to manage critical-path dependencies and rapidly emerging risks.
Document approval
Set shortened review windows, concurrent review, version control and deemed escalation where reviewers miss deadlines. Silence should not constitute approval for material matters.
Programme documents often need input from several functions; unmanaged review cycles create critical-path delay.
Assurance and audit
Move from periodic assurance to risk-based, concurrent assurance focused on governance, controls, testing, migration, cutover and evidence.
Identifying control failures after completion is too late; assurance must influence readiness decisions while remediation remains possible.

Absa · M&A Capability Hub
What is the M&A Capability Hub?
A single source of truth for information on how to execute M&A transactions, to enable scalability and repeatability
The Hub provides the common framework for delivering Absa acquisitions and divestments: a central execution hub, clear functional ownership and partner capacity that scales with transaction demand.
Read the full Vision
What's inside
Everything needed to run an Absa transaction, in one place
The six deal archetypes and their end-to-end lifecycles, the Hub & Spoke operating model with named functional owners, a Partner Accelerator for extra capacity, a mobilisation roadmap and role-based training pathways.
Why Absa needs it
Inorganic growth is central to Absa's strategy
Absa's strategy is increasingly focused on growth across Africa, with inorganic activity expected to form an important part of that ambition. As the volume and complexity of transactions increase, successful delivery will depend on the broader Absa organisation being able to mobilise around deals — not just the central M&A team.

title: Page copy — /mobilisation
text:
[Day11Calendar]
09:00–10:00 — Executive Sponsor all hands
The Executive Sponsor / Accountable Exec holds an all hands meeting for every programme member onboarded thus far, it includes:
A welcome message, thanking everyone for being part of the transaction and raising morale
A recap of the transaction, with a focus on its objectives and outcomes for Absa
A reminder of the governance structures, and roles and responsibilities
A reminder of the rules of engagement
10:00–12:00 — Planning introduction
The Transaction Director and Programme Manager lead a session to kick off the planning phase which includes:
The date for a joint planning workshop to come, and its objectives
The activity required to get to this planning workshop, including introducing and defining deadlines for workstream charters, workstream bricks and workstream blueprints
Milestone creation guidelines, and how the above deliverables support these
How the joint planning workshop will run
Key points of contact for planning
12:00–13:00 — Lunch
13:00–15:00 — Joint workstream planning
Each workstream and their counterparty counterpart jointly discuss planning activities including:
Scheduling regular joint connect sessions
Beginning to define workstream bricks
Setting joint deadlines for bricks and blueprints completion
Discuss key nuances, and surface any major dependencies and differences between buyer and seller
15:00–16:00 — Playback and wrap up
Central Hub leads a wrap up of the day's activities, and plays back the key activities and deadlines for the workstreams.

The vision
A sustainable, scalable and repeatable way of delivering deals
Why Absa needs this capability, what it changes, what it enables, and how to explore it.
Broader Absa context
Inorganic growth is a major focus of Absa's strategy
Absa's strategy is increasingly focused on growth across Africa, with inorganic activity expected to form an important part of that ambition. Acquisitions and divestments are a key lever for entering new markets, building scale and reshaping the portfolio. This M&A Capability Hub is being built to respond to this demand, and enable Absa to execute on this strategy.
A growing pipeline of transactions
As inorganic growth becomes more central to the strategy, Absa expects a greater volume of transactions, of increasing size and complexity, across more markets.
Delivering this ambition requires a sustainable, scalable and repeatable way of executing M&A — which the Capability Hub is designed to provide.
The current challenge
From experience-led delivery to an institutional execution capability

title: Add two geography questions to the Deal Intake Assessment

text:
# Add two geography questions to the Deal Intake Assessment

Two new questions are added at the end of every question path (both Acquisition and Divestment), after the existing final question.

title: Add two geography questions to the Deal Intake Assessment › New questions
breadcrumb: Add two geography questions to the Deal Intake Assessment
text:
## New questions

1. **What is the geographical scope of the deal?**
   - Single geography — the deal is confined to one geography
   - Multi-geography — the deal spans more than one geography

2. **How complex is the regulatory landscape of the geographies involved?**
   - Simple — existing regulator relationships, single regulator, clear expectations and requirements
   - Complex — multi-regulator, opaque regulatory landscape, minimal existing regulator relationships

Both are asked on every branch (no conditional logic), and both are required before results can be viewed.

title: Add two geography questions to the Deal Intake Assessment › Complexity logic
breadcrumb: Add two geography questions to the Deal Intake Assessment
text:
## Complexity logic

- Single geography: no change. Multi-geography: complexity +1.
- Simple regulatory landscape: no change. Complex: complexity +1.

Each uplift adds a named driver to the "What raised the complexity rating" list on the results page:
- "Deal spans multiple geographies"
- "Complex regulatory landscape across the geographies involved"

Complexity still caps at Very high. Deal archetype and deal factors are unaffected.

title: Workstream Centralisation Logic page › The page
text:
## The page

Absa-branded, same header, breadcrumb and back-to-operating-model toolbar as the other operating model pages.

### Decision tree (visual)

Three questions in sequence, each with a "No" branch that ends in "Kept separate":

```text
1. Is centralisation of this workstream likely to be legally allowed?
        | No  -> Kept separate
        v Yes
2. Is centralisation of this workstream within the spirit of the rules?
        | No  -> Kept separate
        v Yes
3. Is there material execution benefit to centralising this workstream?
        | No  -> Kept separate
        v Yes
   Centralised
```

Rendered as stacked question panels with maroon styling, a downward "Yes" path and a side "No" path into a muted "Kept separate" outcome chip; the final "Yes" leads to a filled maroon "Centralised" outcome.

### Assessment table

One row per workstream, one column per question, using a tick, cross or question mark (with accessible text labels):

| Workstream | Q1 legally allowed | Q2 spirit of the rules | Q3 material execution benefit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Comms & Marketing | tick | tick | tick |
| Finance & Tax | tick | ? | ? |
| Compliance | cross | cross | cross |
| Procurement | tick | tick | tick |
| Operations & Servicing | tick | tick | cross |
| Product | cross | cross | tick |
| Risk | cross | cross | cross |
| Data | merged across the three columns with the commentary below | | |
| Technology | tick | tick | tick |

text:
Data row commentary (verbatim): "There may be benefit to centralising a ring-fenced data migration team, but consideration should be given to whether they would be able to have the requisite interaction with business to properly map and build a migration solution"

A small legend above the table explains tick / cross / question mark.
